Methods. This study used a qualitative design. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with thirteen adults (10 women; ages 36 to 61; 13 to 24 months post-stroke). 
Results. A content analysis revealed that person-related factors included the presence and intensity of post-stroke symptoms, self-awareness and readiness to RTW, coping strategies, motivation, financial and social resources, and personal characteristics. Workplace factors included formal and informal accommodations, interpersonal aspects and employment conditions. Factors related to health services included adapted medical accommodations and medical follow-up, access to supportive care services (functional and psychological support), as well as recognition of patient’s condition and needs. 
Conclusions. The study confirms certain factors proposed in the existing literature, highlighting those specific to a population that often present fewer post-stroke impairments and rarely receives rehabilitation services. All these factors must be considered to provide more appropriate healthcare services, to guide workplaces in the type of support they can offer, and to assist individual in their recovery and RTW following a mild stroke.

articles.title: Cardio-respiratory modulation of arousal and excitability states
articles.authors: Teresa Berther; Martina Saltafossi; Daniel Kluger
articles.abstract: The field of interoception research is currently working towards an understanding of how brain-body states determine human perception, cognition, and behaviour. Recent studies suggest that transient dynamics of arousal neuromodulation and cortical excitability are of particular interest. In this Perspective Article, we succinctly review the current evidence for cardio-respiratory modulation of arousal and excitability states in the human brain. We outline the systematic relationships of both cardiac and respiratory rhythms to non-invasive readouts such as changes in pupil diameter as well as (a)periodic neural signatures of excitability. Integrating these single-domain findings, we suggest a path towards a multi-organ perspective of brain-body neuroscience.

articles.title: Introducing openESM: A database of openly available experience sampling datasets
articles.authors: Björn S. Siepe; Jonas M B Haslbeck; Matthias Kloft; Anabel Büchner; Yong Zhang; Eiko I Fried; Daniel W. Heck
articles.abstract: Experience sampling via mobile devices enables unprecedented insights into daily life. However, individual studies often cannot answer research questions conclusively, and open data are scattered across repositories in different formats. This impedes research into robustness, generalizability, and heterogeneity. We address this issue by introducing openESM, an open-source database of openly available experience sampling datasets in a harmonized format. The growing database currently comprises 60 datasets with more than 16,000 participants and more than 740,000 observations. Metadata can be searched via our website (openesmdata.org) to select and download datasets via packages in R and Python. We demonstrate the potential of openESM through an analysis of within-person correlations of positive and negative affect in 39 datasets, providing evidence for a large negative momentary correlation (-0.49, 95% CI: [-0.54, -0.42]). We end by discussing the design principles that will allow openESM to become a continuously evolving community resource for cumulative experience sampling research.

articles.title: BoundIRT: An R Package for Bounded Continuous Item Response Theory with Factor Score Regression
articles.authors: Dylan Molenaar
articles.abstract: In various research settings, responses to questionnaire items are continuously distributed and bounded from below and above. Suitable item response theory (IRT) models are available for the response data; however, implementations of these models differ significantly in their estimation method, availability, and user-friendliness. These differences hamper the application of such models in general, and model fit comparison in particular. Therefore, in this paper, BoundIRT is presented, which implements four popular bounded IRT models from the literature in the R statistical computing environment. The package provides various facilities for model estimation and model fit assessment. In addition, once a suitable model has been established for a given dataset, the factor score regression facilities can be used to conduct regression analyses of the latent variable in the model with respect to other variables.

articles.title: Shared Reality, Perceived Responsiveness and Interpersonal Emotion Regulation Among Parents-Adolescents Dyads
articles.authors: Roni Yuval; Reuma Gadassi Polack; Hadas Wiseman; Haran Sened
articles.abstract: Shared reality is an experience of having "merged minds" and shared inner states, e.g. feelings, thoughts, opinions and concerns with a close relationship partner. It is a substantial component for establishing and nurturing close relationships. The purpose of this study was to examine, for the first time, shared reality between parents and children. To this day, the focus of research in this field was on romantic couples and adult strangers. We investigated 60 dyads of parents of adolescent children (ages 9-17) through self-report questionnaires and experience sampling methods, completed by parents 3 times a day for 3 days (K=728 questionnaires). Stronger parent-child shared reality was found to be associated with more perceived responsiveness experienced by the parent from the child, and with more interpersonal emotion regulation behaviors performed by the parent towards the child. The associations remained when controlling for parent-child closeness and for parent shared reality with their partner. Together, these findings suggest that shared reality is a significant and valuable factor within parent-adolescent relationships, with unique relevance beyond other relationship components. Our findings demonstrate how the unique shared reality between children and parents can be an essential part of the family’s everyday life.

articles.title: Cognitive maps are flexible, dynamic, (re)constructed representations
articles.authors: Aidan J Horner; James A. Ainge; Alexander Easton; Simon J James; Jeremy Kendal; John Sutton; Jan Wiener
articles.abstract: Spatial navigation is the ability to purposefully move from one location to another. Central to many theories of navigation is the proposal that we build a ‘cognitive map’ of our external environment. We identify three conceptions of cognitive maps, from highly coherent long-term representations of space to more fragmentary representations. Reviewing the literature, we show that many navigation behaviours thought to require a cognitive map can be supported by the interaction of specific navigation strategies with minimal, fragmentary knowledge of the environment. Further, we argue that the range of navigation behaviours, strategies, individual differences, and navigational aids and systems used during navigation point toward representations that are more flexible than any of the three main conceptions of a cognitive map allow. We propose that spatial knowledge is stored in a more fragmentary manner but, critically, more complex representations are (re)constructed dynamically in the given navigational moment. The form and complexity of these constructed representations are tightly connected to the dynamic interaction between the navigator, including the strategies and aids they are using, and the environment. We link this proposal to the literature on spatially tuned neurons in the medial temporal lobes, emphasising that the heterogeneity of these functional neurons and their adaptation to changes in environmental structure and navigational goals supports our proposal that cognitive maps are dynamically (re)constructed representations. Therefore, cognitive maps are not relatively coherent, stable representations of spatial environments, but instead are dynamically and flexibly (re)constructed representations of the given navigational moment.

articles.title: The Association Between SES and Students’ Achievement Motivation in Secondary School: An Individual Participant Data Meta-Analysis Spanning Two Decades of PISA Data
articles.authors: Sarah Grünthal; Lena Keller; Julia Kretschmann; Hanna Dumont; Martin Brunner
articles.abstract: Major theoretical frameworks of achievement motivation link family socioeconomic status (SES) to students’ achievement motivation in school settings. However, systematic evidence on this association remains limited. This study presents the first meta-analysis on this topic, using representative individual participant data (IPD) from the Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA). The analysis included 485 student samples comprising a total of 3,576,278 15-year-old students, spanning four SES indicators, eight achievement motivation components, four academic domains, 92 countries, and eight assessment cycles across more than two decades (2000–2022). The average meta-analytic association between SES and achievement motivation was small (r = .10, 95% CI [.09, .11]), indicating slightly higher achievement motivation among students from higher-SES families. The magnitude of the association varied meaningfully across SES indicators and motivational components, but only marginally across academic domains. Educational home resources (e.g., books, educational materials) showed stronger associations with achievement motivation than parental education or occupational status, and self-efficacy exhibited the largest association among motivational components. The association increased over historical time but declined following the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic. After controlling for academic achievement, the meta-analytic average association between family SES and achievement motivation remained statistically significant, but its magnitude was attenuated. These nuanced findings highlight the complex association between family SES and students’ achievement motivation, emphasizing the multidimensionality of both constructs and providing an important empirical foundation for evaluating, refining, and advancing psychological theories that address the link between family SES and students’ achievement motivation.

articles.title: In drones we trust!?  Insights into mental model formation, trust development, and behavioral outcomes in autonomous technology: The case of human-drone interaction
articles.authors: Lisa Thomaschewski; Markus Pauly; Olga Vogel; Sven Franke; Christopher Reining; Shrutarv Awasthi; Annette Kluge
articles.abstract: As autonomous drones become increasingly integrated into intralogistics warehousing environments, understanding how trust develops in these systems is critical. This study investigates how brief interaction with an autonomous drone influences users’ mental models, trust, behavior, and semantic representations. Nineteen participants interacted with a drone in a warehouse mock-up. Measures were collected before, during, immediately after, and two to three weeks post-interaction. Mental model accuracy improved and remained stable at follow-up. Intention to use and several generalized trust dimensions increased over time, whereas situational trust and comfort proximity remained unchanged. Exploratory analyses indicated a positive association between higher post-interaction mental model accuracy and generalized trust at follow-up. Semantic representations remained primarily technical-functional across measurement-points. Together, the findings suggest a temporally delayed relationship between mental model updating and trust formation, indicating that interaction may shape trust through the development of increasingly accurate mental representations of autonomous systems rather than increasingly anthropomorphic representations.

articles.title: Sampling from Implicit Bayesian Models: Towards a General Framework for Cognitive Modeling
articles.authors: Haijiang Yan; Jenny Zhou; Yitong Lin; Nick Chater; Adam N Sanborn
articles.abstract: Computational process models are pivotal tools for studying the human mind, offering explicit algorithmic accounts of how human behavior arises. However, they are often siloed across individual tasks and domains, lacking a coherent framework for examining computational principles shared across cognition. The challenges are twofold. First, existing models rely heavily on researcher-defined and task-dependent representations of the stimuli. Second, they typically capture only a limited range of behavioral responses. To address these limitations, we propose a two-component framework. A neural network, trained on ecologically valid ground-truth data, functions as an Implicit Bayesian Model (IBM) that maps complex real-world stimuli directly onto posterior probability distributions. A human-like sampling process, the Autocorrelated Bayesian Sampler (ABS), then samples hypotheses from those posteriors to generate diverse behavioral responses while accounting for systematic deviations from normative predictions. This combination of realistic representations with a general-purpose algorithmic decision process enables cognitive mechanisms to be implemented and transferred across tasks at real-world scale. Through three case studies spanning multiple domains and stimulus modalities, we demonstrate the generality of the IBM-ABS framework in explaining human behavior both qualitatively and quantitatively, and explore its capacity to yield new theoretical insights through incorporating realistic priors and predicting the effects of experimental manipulations.

articles.title: Auditory Function Following Sport-Related Concussion And Repetitive Head Impacts: A Scoping Review
articles.authors: Ewan Dean; Jessica Rose Andrew; John Oyewole; Christopher Gaffney; Kate Slade; Helen Nuttall
articles.abstract: Sport-related head impacts are common in contact sports, and resulting auditory symptoms, such as difficulty understanding speech-in-noise, are frequently reported. Yet auditory function remains absent from concussion assessment protocols. Repetitive head impacts are linked to neurodegenerative diseases, highlighting the need for sensitive, accessible biomarkers. Auditory processing relies on precisely timed subcortical and cortical neural transmission, making it vulnerable to diffuse axonal injury and the neurometabolic cascade of concussion. Further, the auditory cortex lies within the lateral sulcus, a region highly vulnerable to concussive impacts. This vulnerability suggests auditory measures may provide a window into concussion-related neuropathology. To explore how sports-related head impacts affect auditory function, a JBI and PRISMA-ScR-compliant scoping review was conducted. MEDLINE, PsycINFO, Embase, SPORTDiscus and grey literature were searched from inception to March 2026. Eligible studies assessed auditory function in athletes following concussive, sub-concussive, or repetitive head impacts in sport. Thirty-one studies met criteria. Peripheral hearing remained within clinically normal limits (across frequencies 0.25-8 kHz), yet central auditory processing deficits emerged within hours to years’ post-concussion. Subcortically, speech-evoked frequency following responses showed reduced fundamental frequency amplitude. Cortically, N100 amplitude reductions suggest early disruption of auditory processing. Higher-order auditory function, measured with auditory oddball paradigms, demonstrated reduced P300 amplitude, even after symptoms had resolved. Contact sport participation was also associated with poorer speech-in-noise performance and elevated rates of tinnitus and noise sensitivity. Despite converging electrophysiological evidence and a physiologically motivated rationale, auditory assessment remains absent from concussion management. While gaps remain, including limited data on female, elite, and retired athletes, the auditory system represents an underutilised biomarker of concussion-related neuropathology with implications for monitoring brain health and protecting athletes’ perceptual and communication abilities.

articles.title: Are agreement attraction errors processed in the same way across bilinguals' languages? Insights from bilingual speakers of non-standard varieties in Italy
articles.authors: Camilla Masullo; Alba Casado; Beatrice Giustolisi; Evelina Leivada
articles.abstract: Studying how bilingual populations compute grammatical illusions sheds light on how variables such as language use and practices impact language processing. Although encompassing variation in language of testing and bilingual profile can further clarify the role of such variables, studies tend to focus on only one of bilinguals’ languages and consider bilingual groups speaking a limited set of standard language pairs. By adopting a two-way comparative perspective, we investigate how Subject-Verb agreement mismatches are processed in two non-standard language bilingual communities of Italy, namely Italian-Agrigentino (n = 24) and Italian-Pavese (n = 23) bilinguals. Despite both being characterized by the coexistence of a standard and non-standard linguistic variety, each community presents unique sociolinguistic ecologies in terms of linguistic habits. Participants did an auditory acceptability judgement task with sentences with incorrect Subject-Verb agreement as stimuli. The same sentence was presented in Italian and either Agrigentino or Pavese according to the bilingual group, aiming to run a between-language comparison and observe whether the (non) standard status of a language influences processing outcomes. Judgements were elicited on a 5-point Likert scale and reaction times were recorded.  Both bilingual groups gave higher acceptability ratings to ungrammatical stimuli in Italian compared to the non-standard language, meaning that they better spotted agreement mismatches in the standard variety. Yet, Italian-Agrigentino bilinguals were faster in judging stimuli in their non-standard language compared to Italian, while Italian-Pavese bilinguals showed the opposite trend. Other between-group differences concerned both the type of sociolinguistic factor modulating processing outcomes, such as the amount of non-standard language use and switching, and the way in which these factors played a role. Our results suggest that appreciating variation in both the language of testing and bilingual phenotype is crucial when examining bilingual language processing, especially in contexts of non-standard language bilingualism.

articles.title: WordSeg: Standardizing unsupervised word form segmentation from text
articles.authors: Alex Eguiluz; mathieu bernard; Roland Thiolliere; Amanda Saksida; Georgia Loukatou; Elin Larsen; Mark Johnson; Laia Fibla; Emmanuel Dupoux; Robert Daland
articles.abstract: A basic task in language acquisition likely involves discovering the boundaries between words or morphemes in input where these basic units are not overtly segmented. A number of unsupervised learning algorithms have been proposed in the last 20 years for these purposes, some of which have been implemented computationally and made publicly available. The present paper presents a suite that integrates an array of algorithms, and systematizes the set of steps involved in word segmentation studies, including an evaluation procedure. We illustrate the use of this package by analyzing a corpus of child-directed speech in various ways, which further allows us to make recommendations for experimental design of follow-up work. We conclude by outlining fruitful directions for further development.

articles.title: UnfoldBIDS.jl: Streamlining regression ERP Analysis of BIDS-Compliant EEG Data in Julia
articles.authors: Skukies René; Benedikt Valerian Ehinger
articles.abstract:
The increasing complexity of naturalistic experiments requires advanced analytical methods, with the regression-based event-related potential (rERP) framework emerging as a promising tool for flexible, single-trial EEG analysis. Alongside methodological progress, the Brain Imaging Data Structure (BIDS) has revolutionized data sharing by standardizing file organization and enabling seamless integration across tools and pipelines. However, bridging these advancements, rERP modeling and BIDS-compliant datasets, typically requires cumbersome custom scripting, limiting reproducibility and efficiency.
  Here, we introduce UnfoldBIDS.jl, a Julia package that integrates BIDS-structured datasets with the rERP capabilities of Unfold.jl, streamlining the analysis of large-scale EEG datasets. The package simplifies analyses of BIDS-datasets, allows for preprocessing using MNE-python, returns tidy datasets for visualization or further statistical analysis and includes both documentation and tutorials.

articles.title: Not so average: Heterogeneous boredom dynamics during an incremental physical effort task
articles.authors: Katja Rewitz; Wanja Wolff; Maik Bieleke
articles.abstract:
Boredom is a dynamic state that promotes task disengagement and behavioral change. Despite the centrality of temporal dynamics in boredom conceptualizations, little empirical work has examined how it unfolds during sustained performance and how these dynamics relate to behavior. Here, we tracked boredom, alongside physical and cognitive effort, throughout an incremental cycling task performed until voluntary disengagement, and decomposed individual trajectories using functional principal component analysis (fPCA). Whereas physical and cognitive effort increased largely uniformly, boredom showed pronounced interindividual variability in boredom levels and temporal trends. Boredom trend, but not boredom level predicted performance: greater alignment with 
decreasing (rather than increasing) boredom trends predicted longer persistence, even after controlling for perceived physical and cognitive effort. Thus, this study offers initial empirical evidence that boredom is not an ‘average’ experience but a dynamic process whose unfolding varies systematically across individuals and relates to task persistence. Tracking such dynamics illustrates how temporal modeling can advance the understanding and theoretical treatment of how boredom shapes task engagement.

articles.title: What’s a multiverse good for anyway?
articles.authors: Julia M. Rohrer; Jessica Hullman; Andrew Gelman
articles.abstract: Multiverse analysis has become a fairly popular approach, as indicated by the present special issue on the matter. Here, we take one step back and ask why one would conduct a multiverse analysis in the first place. We discuss various ways in which a multiverse may be employed – as a tool for reflection and critique, as a persuasive tool, as a serious inferential tool – as well as potential problems that arise depending on the specific purpose. For example, it fails as a persuasive tool when researchers disagree about which variations should be included in the analysis, and it fails as a serious inferential tool when the included analyses do not target a coherent estimand. Then, we take yet another step back and ask what the multiverse discourse has been good for and whether any broader lessons can be drawn. Ultimately, we conclude that the multiverse does remain a valuable tool; however, we urge against taking it too seriously.

articles.title: High/Low-Context Communication: (Re)conceptualization and Measurement
articles.authors: Joep Hofhuis; Lily A. Arasaratnam-Smith
articles.abstract: High/low-context communication (HLCC) is one of the most widely used concepts in intercultural communication, yet little theoretical development has taken place over the past decades and existing measurement instruments remain psychometrically and theoretically limited. We argue that prior operationalizations have captured only a subset of the construct's theoretical scope, and propose a reconceptualization of HLCC as a multidimensional individual-level orientation encompassing four core dimensions: verbal vs. nonverbal communication, honesty vs. relationship orientation, self-awareness, and shared understanding. We report two studies documenting the development and validation of the High/Low-Context Communication Scale (HLCCS). Study 1 (n = 276) established the factor structure and initial validity. Study 2 (n = 576) confirmed measurement invariance across six culturally diverse nations (Netherlands, USA, UK, South Africa, India, Japan), and provided convergent and discriminant validity evidence against individualism/collectivism and social dominance orientation. The HLCCS offers a theoretically grounded and psychometrically sound instrument for individual-level assessment of communication style.

articles.title: Embodied Grounding as a Mechanism Linking Personality Organization to Behavioural Regulation
articles.authors: Salvatore Manuel Diana; MARTINA CILIBERTI; Laura Barca
articles.abstract: Recent theoretical accounts propose that body-oriented behaviours reflect a broader organizational process through which individuals regulate internal states and preserve self-coherence. The present study investigated whether the broader organizational architecture underlying this account is already detectable within a non-clinical population. Specifically, we examined whether personality organization influences behavioural vulnerability through embodied grounding. A community sample completed questionnaires assessing personality organization, interoceptive experience, bodily identity, intolerance of uncertainty, and eating-related vulnerability. Structural equation modelling showed that, within a non-clinical population, the association between personality organization and eating-related vulnerability was fully mediated by embodied dimensions. Interoceptive trust emerged as the strongest protective factor, whereas bodily identity fragility represented the principal pathway linking personality organization to behavioural vulnerability. Although bodily identity strongly predicted intolerance of uncertainty, intolerance of uncertainty did not independently contribute to eating-related vulnerability once embodied dimensions were taken into account. Rather than identifying a mechanism specific to eating behaviour, these findings suggest that embodied grounding constitutes a general organizational process through which stable modes of personality organization become translated into behavioural regulation.

articles.title: Sample Size Requirements for Continuous Norms: Two Illustrative Examples
articles.authors: Julian Urban; Vsevolod Scherrer; Franzis Preckel
articles.abstract: Precise norm scores are essential for psychological diagnostics. While conventional norming estimates norms within subgroups, continuous norming uses regression to estimate norms based on the entire sample. Consequently, continuous norming should provide sufficient precision with smaller sample sizes than conventional norming. However, clear insights on the sample sizes required to achieve sufficient precision for continuous norming are scarce. To provide empirical insights into the required sample sizes of continuous norming, we present two illustrative examples using normative data from two intelligence tests to evaluate the precision of continuous norms across varying sample sizes, norm predictor values, and ability levels. Our examples show that continuous norming achieves a sufficient precision with substantially smaller samples than conventional norming (N = 1,000–1,500 vs. N = 2,500–3,000). However, precision declines at extreme percentiles and norm predictor values, emphasizing the need to tailor sample size planning to the specific test and its use.

articles.title: Introducing GenAI to assessment in Higher Education risks the social contract between staff and students: a qualitative study
articles.authors: Lyba Razzaq; Isla Fay; Deborah Talmi; Roni Tibon; Maryam Abo-Tabik; Alexandru Marcoci; Giulio Corsi; Sarah N. Mattey; Georgiana Thorpe-Apreutesei; Yael Benn
articles.abstract: While perspectives on the use of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) in assessment in higher education have been widely reported, less is known about discipline-specific concern. Here we focus on Psychology, where essays are central to assessment and require context-dependent judgement, critical evaluation, synthesis of evidence, and scientific reasoning. To ensure that findings reflect shared, cross-institution concerns in this discipline, we conducted semi-structured focus groups with Psychology students (N = 11) and staff (N = 14) from three UK universities differing in geographical location and entry-requirements. Discussions explored views on GenAI in HE for assessment, including reactions to examples comparing human and AI-generated feedback. Thematic analysis identified three themes: (1) Human-Machine Ambiguity, (2) Overreliance, Weakening Cognition and the Value of Education, and (3) The Social Contract: Personal and Interpersonal Values. Consistent with previous research, participants raised concerns about ethics, fairness, data integrity, and the impact on learning and cognition. Extending existing literature, findings highlight concerns about the erosion of trust and the social contract underpinning higher education, which could threaten the experience of staff and students. With its focus on essays in assessment, psychology provides a strong test case for examining the views of staff and students on AI-grading more generally.

articles.title: Measuring Forecasting Proficiency: A Psychometric Perspective
articles.authors: Fabio Setti; Leah Feuerstahler; Sophie Ma Zhu; Nikolay Petrov; Ezra Karger; Mark Himmelstein
articles.abstract: Identifying good forecasters, individuals who consistently make accurate predictions about future events, is one central research topic in the forecasting literature. One of the latest developments in this stream of research is the Forecasting Proficiency Test (FPT), which aims to provide a reliable and accessible measure of individual forecasting ability. A large portion of the FPT consists of quantile elicitation format (QEF) forecasts rather than the more common probability elicitation format (PEF). We propose a novel psychometric model that draws upon item response theory, with the goal of measuring item features of QEF items and capturing individual forecasting ability as a latent construct. In doing so, we outline important theoretical differences between latent constructs and accuracy metrics commonly employed in the forecasting literature to measure forecasting proficiency. We demonstrate the practical usefulness of the proposed model by applying it to the QEF questions of the FPT, where we find that it captures meaningful item features and adequately measures forecasting ability. Namely, the estimated latent construct forecasting ability showed a Pearson correlation of r = .85 with measures based on strictly proper scoring rules of forecasting accuracy. We conclude by discussing the practical benefits of measuring item parameters of forecasting items, the specific limitations of psychometric models applied to forecasting items, and when and where we believe they are most appropriate in the forecasting domain.

articles.title: Active sampling helps children learn new words by tuning their curriculum to past experiences
articles.authors: Martin Zettersten; Koeun Choi; Heather Kirkorian; Jenny Saffran
articles.abstract: Young children are actively engaged in structuring their early language learning. But what sampling preferences do children have when actively seeking new information about unfamiliar words? And when and why is active control beneficial for learning words? Across 2 experiments (N = 303; M(age) = 4.6 years; range: 3.0-6.0; 166 female, 137 male; 85.8% White, 5.6% more than one race, 2.6% Asian, 0.7% Black; 6.2% Hispanic or Latino), we manipulated whether 3- to 5-year-old children were able to actively select their word learning input or were passively exposed to the active selections of another child. Experiment 1 used a yoked active-passive design. We found that having active control did not benefit children’s learning of unfamiliar novel words relative to receiving that same input passively. In Experiment 2, we first gave children experience with novel words, such that some object-label associations were experienced more frequently than others. Children who had active control systematically made more informative choices by selecting less frequently experienced object-label associations. By comparing their performance to children in two different passive conditions, we showed that children learn novel words better when experiencing input tuned to their past experience, regardless of whether they actively select this input themselves or passively experience the choices of a child sharing their same past word learning experience. Together, these studies demonstrate when and how active information-seeking benefits children’s word learning.

articles.title: Children resolving spoken mispronunciations: The role of sentence context
articles.authors: Signy Wegener; Rauno Parrila; Laura Steacy; Danielle Colenbrander; Valeria Maria Rigobon; Louise Keun; Noam Siegelman; Saskia Kohnen; Elisabeth Beyersmann; Lyndall Murray
articles.abstract: Purpose: Theories of set for variability identify a role for sentence context within the process of resolving mispronunciations during reading (Share, 1995; Venezky, 1999), yet prior work has focused on mispronunciations of isolated spoken words. The primary aim of the current study was to examine whether sentence context boosted correction accuracy, compared to isolated mispronunciations, and to what extent this benefit derived from syntactic and semantic support. A secondary aim was to better understand the mispronunciation correction process by examining predictors of correction success. Finally, correlations explored the relationship between the mispronunciation correction tasks and standardised reading and letter-sound measures. Method: Sixty-two Year 1 children completed three oral mispronunciation correction conditions: isolated mispronunciations; mispronunciations that followed syntactically supportive sentences; and mispronunciations that followed syntactically and semantically supportive sentences. Child-, word- and child-by-word measures were also administered. Results: A logistic linear mixed effects model predicting correction accuracy revealed better performance when context was present than when it was absent, and a small but significant benefit of greater semantic support from context. Accuracy was predicted by features at the child- (word reading), word- (transparency rating; frequency), and importantly, at the child-by-word levels (item-specific reading, lexical phonology and semantic knowledge). Compared to the isolated and syntactic conditions, syntactically and semantically supportive contexts exhibited a weaker relationship with word reading. Conclusion: Context assists with correcting mispronunciations, pointing especially to an enhancing role of semantic support, and supporting the existence of a direct relationship between item-specific word knowledge and mispronunciation correction success.

articles.title: How Norm Information on Cable News Shapes Second-Order Beliefs About Democratic Practices
articles.authors: Jordana Composto; Kristopher L. Nichols; Elke U. Weber
articles.abstract: Support for democratic norms among Americans is strong, yet most believe their fellow citizens are abandoning these values. Such misperceptions are consequential, as second-order beliefs about what others support shape willingness to accept or even endorse violations of democratic practice. We examine how partisan cable news shapes these second-order beliefs in two ways. Using fine-tuned large language models to analyze two months of MSNBC, CNN, and Fox News coverage (3,265 hours of programming) preceding the 2024 presidential election, the first large-scale quantification of norm content in a naturalistic media environment. We show that norm information pervades coverage of democratic practices and is accurately calibrated to actual public opinion on MSNBC and CNN, though not on Fox News. Two preregistered experiments then reveal detection-dependence: exposure to norm information shifts second-order beliefs only when viewers detect it as such. Once detected, viewers whose political ideology is aligned with the channel broadcasting the message update their second-order beliefs toward the norm message, whereas misaligned viewers move away from it in reactance, in both cases leaving first-order attitudes unchanged. This detection-dependent, match-moderated mechanism explains how identical normative content corrects some viewers’ misperceptions while distorting others’, sustaining false polarization about democratic conduct even when underlying values have not changed.

articles.title: Practice Effects Confound the Emotion–Performance Link in Self-Regulated Learning: A Reanalysis of Lin et al. (2026)
articles.authors: Chi Zhang
articles.abstract: Lin et al. (*Journal of Educational Psychology*, 2026) proposed a computational model of the dynamic interplay between goal setting, performance, and emotions in self-regulated learning. In a repetitive math task (Study 1), they reported that positive emotions predicted lower subsequent performance, interpreting this via the coasting hypothesis. We argue that this finding may instead reflect a temporal confound: in a repetitive task, performance improves due to practice while emotional engagement declines, producing a spurious negative association when time trends are unmodeled. We reanalyze the Study 1 data by introducing a log(trial) learning curve into the best-fitting model. The negative emotion-to-performance effect is no longer credible in this extended model; instead, a strong practice effect emerges. This confound-based interpretation also parsimoniously accounts for why the emotion-to-performance pathway reversed direction in the original Study 2, where task variety and high stakes attenuate practice-driven time trends. Methodologically, we show that the WAIC criterion used in the original study exhibits poor diagnostic reliability and is theoretically biased for autoregressive panel models. We implement exact leave-future-out cross-validation as an unbiased alternative, under which the original model selection conclusions are no longer supported.

articles.title: Comparative efficacy of CBT protocols with different behavioral techniques for procrastination: a randomized controlled trial
articles.authors: Weronika Maria Browarczyk; Joachim Kowalski; Magdalena Pietruch; Justyna Piwińska; Marek Wypych; Jarosław M. Michałowski
articles.abstract:
Introduction. Procrastination is highly prevalent among university students, often becoming chronic and undermining academic performance and well-being. Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is the most studied treatment, but evidence remains limited to a few rigorous trials, broad multi-component packages, and scarce long-term follow-up. We evaluated two CBT protocols differing in behavioral modules against an active comparator and waitlist control.

Methods. In this four-arm randomized controlled trial, 255 help-seeking university students with problematic procrastination, verified through semi-structured clinical interviews, were randomized to Realistic Planning and Timely Beginning (RPT), Working Time Restriction (WTR), the Pomodoro Technique (PT), or waitlist (WL). Active conditions comprised five weekly online group sessions with shared psychoeducational and cognitive modules. Outcomes included academic procrastination (API-R), three Pure Procrastination Scale subscales, academic project progress, depression (PHQ-9), anxiety (GAD-7), and treatment-attributed negative effects (NEQ-20), analyzed using linear mixed models, with a six-month follow-up in active conditions.

Results. All active interventions produced large reductions in procrastination compared with WL (API-R: d = −1.24 to −1.54), with no significant differences between them. Reliable or likely improvement occurred in 44.8–55.4% of active-condition participants versus 15.5% in WL. RPT and WTR additionally improved project progress. Depression decreased in all active conditions and anxiety in WTR and PT. Procrastination reductions were maintained at six months; early gains in depression and anxiety were not. Negative effects, reported by 39.7% of completers, were mostly mild or moderate.

Conclusion. Brief group-based CBT protocols produced large and durable reductions in problematic procrastination among university students, with comparable efficacy across protocols.

articles.title: Not enjoyable, but meaningful: A qualitative thematic analysis exploring internalisation and autonomous motivation in unassisted smoking cessation
articles.authors: Effie Marathia; Sheila Duffy; Blair Saunders
articles.abstract:
Objectives: This study explored how successful unassisted quitters described their motivations for quitting, with particular attention to whether external antecedents, including health-related events, social expectations, and financial pressures, became internalised into more self-endorsed reasons for quitting.
Design: Qualitative interview study using reflexive thematic analysis.
Methods: Thirty-two adults living in Scotland who had quit smoking unassisted between six months and ten years prior to participation took part in semi-structured interviews. Interviews explored participants’ experiences of quitting without formal support, including what motivated their quit attempt. Data were analysed inductively using reflexive thematic analysis, informed by Self-determination Theory and the Health Belief Model. 
Results: Four themes were developed: Brushing with Mortality, Quitting for More than Me, A Life Beyond Smoking, and Counting the Cost. Participants described quitting as prompted by health crises, social roles, a desire for autonomy, future aspirations, and financial pressures. These motivations were rarely experienced as purely internal or external. Instead, participants’ accounts suggested a process of internalisation, whereby externally prompted concerns became personally meaningful and aligned with valued identities, responsibilities, and desired futures. Intrinsic motivation, understood as quitting because the act itself was inherently enjoyable, was largely absent. 
Conclusions: Unassisted quitting appears to be a relational, identity-based, and future-oriented process. The results suggest that smoking cessation research may benefit from moving beyond binary distinctions between intrinsic and extrinsic motivation and instead focusing on how quitting becomes internalised and integrated into people’s values, identities, and life goals.

articles.title: Individual Differences in Achievement Goal Orientation Predict Neural Responses to Negative Feedback
articles.authors: Darian Raizberg; Samantha DePasque; Valerie Backstrom; Luis M. Rivera; Elizabeth Tricomi
articles.abstract: Negative feedback is seldom welcomed and often avoided. Whether through verbal critiques, poor exam grades, or non-verbal cues, negative feedback is a tool commonly used by educators to identify errors and areas needing improvement. However, negative feedback can induce negative emotions and is known to decrease activity in the ventral striatum (VS), a key structure in the brain’s reward system. Despite this, previous research has shown that VS activation to negative feedback can meaningfully shift based on contextual and motivational factors. In the present study, we sought to determine whether individual differences in approach and avoidance goals are motivational factors that meaningfully shift BOLD responses to feedback in the VS. To this end, following a competence threat, participants completed a word association learning task and received performance related feedback while undergoing fMRI scanning. We found that neural responses to negative feedback were significantly associated with approach goals. More specifically, we found that VS responses to negative feedback, which typically dip below baseline, were less negative for individuals higher in approach goals. These results suggest that individual differences in achievement goals can interact with contextual factors to influence how negative feedback is viewed, whether instructive or punitive, and that these responses can be reflected in the striatum.

articles.title: The Interplay between Math and Reading Anxiety and Academic Skills in Primary School: A Longitudinal Study
articles.authors: Marek Matouš Bula; Daria Khanolainen; Tuire Koponen; Riikka Sorvo; Minna Torppa
articles.abstract: The early school years are a crucial period for the development of foundational mathematics and reading skills, as well as academic anxieties. Understanding how achievement and anxiety are related during this period is essential for supporting children's academic success and well-being. This study examined the early development of mathematics and reading achievement and anxiety and their within- and across-domain associations from Grades 2 to 3. A Finnish sample of 800 children (409 girls) was assessed in Grade 2 (N = 668) and Grade 3 (N = 711) using standardized tests for reading and arithmetic fluency, while self-evaluation questionnaires measured reading and math anxiety. The longitudinal model revealed within-domain stability for reading and arithmetic fluency and for  reading and math anxiety as well as within-domain predictive effects from skill to anxiety. Only one significant positive cross-domain path was found, that from reading fluency to arithmetic fluency. No gender differences were found in the longitudinal associations between skills and anxiety and controlling for parental education or child age did not change the results. The developmental dynamics between anxiety and skill thus appear to run from skills to anxiety and be domain-specific early on.

articles.title: Postpartum Depression and Anxiety: A Literature Review of Neural Mechanisms, Child Outcomes, and Treatment Outcomes
articles.authors: Kayleigh Esparza; Jacob Armstrong; Robin Aupperle
articles.abstract: Background: Postpartum depression (PPD) and postpartum anxiety (PPA) affect approximately 10–20% of mothers worldwide and frequently co-occur, yet growing evidence suggests they may be associated with distinct neural mechanisms, require differential treatment strategies, and have unique impacts on child outcomes. The present review synthesizes findings concerning the neural changes associated with PPD and PPA, how those changes relate to parenting and child outcomes, and the neural mechanisms by which treatment approaches improve outcomes in postpartum mothers. Main Text: Normative neurobiological changes during pregnancy involve hormonal fluctuations in estrogen, progesterone, oxytocin, and prolactin that contribute to gray matter volume reductions in social cognition regions, alongside white matter and functional changes, collectively priming the maternal brain for caregiving. These structural changes partially recover during the postpartum period, with the magnitude of recovery associated with greater parental self-efficacy. Mothers with PPD and PPA show partially distinct neural profiles relative to healthy postpartum mothers. PPD is associated with HPA hyperactivation and elevated cortisol, reduced executive control network connectivity, and mixed salience network disruptions, consistent with its behavioral profile of anhedonia and reduced emotional availability. Research on PPA neurobiology is more limited; however, existing evidence suggests heightened salience network activity, stronger prefrontal-striatal connectivity, and a distinct HPA profile of lower cortisol output, consistent with the heightened negative emotions and anxious caregiving associated with PPA. Regarding treatment, evidence from broader mood and anxiety disorder populations suggests CBT and SSRIs influence neural circuits involved in affective regulation and executive control, while GABA modulators target GABAergic pathways at the receptor level, though direct neuroimaging studies of treatment response in postpartum populations remain absent. Conclusion: PPD and PPA have partially distinct neurobiological underpinnings, potentially requiring unique treatment approaches. Future research is needed to better understand how these neurobiological changes relate longitudinally to maternal mental health and child outcomes and how established treatments impact brain structure and function in postpartum mothers. Advancing this line of research will be important for informing specific targets for prevention and intervention programs.

articles.title: Can Physical Activity Moderate the Association Between Speech-in-Noise Hearing Ability and Cognitive Performance? A UK Biobank Analysis
articles.authors: Jessica Rose Andrew; Andrew Thomas; Chris Plack; Christopher Gaffney; Helen Nuttall
articles.abstract:
Objectives: The present study aimed to determine if objectively measured physical activity moderated the association between speech-in-noise hearing ability and cognitive performance in middle-aged and older adults. Exploratory analyses also examined whether physical activity was associated with social isolation, and whether this association varied according to hearing ability.
Design: A cross-sectional analysis was conducted using data from the UK Biobank cohort. The final descriptive sample included 18,787 participants aged 46 – 85 years, including 10,372 females and 8,415 males. Hearing ability was determined by calculating the better-ear speech reception threshold (SRT) derived from the Digit Triplet Test. Physical activity levels were objectively captured over a continuous seven-day window using wrist-worn accelerometers. Cognitive performance was evaluated using a global cognitive composite score derived via Principal Component Analysis, and social isolation was classified as a binary variable. Multiple linear and binary logistic regression models evaluated primary moderation and exploratory associations, adjusting for age, sex, and educational attainment.
Results: The primary cognitive model included 18,753 participants, and the exploratory social isolation model included 15,703 participants. Higher better-ear SRT was associated with lower cognitive composite scores (B = −0.060, p < .001). Objective physical activity was not associated with cognitive composite scores (B = −0.001, p = .302), and the interaction between objective physical activity and better-ear SRT was not statistically significant (p = .612). In the exploratory models, higher levels of objective physical activity were significantly associated with lower odds of social isolation (B = −0.024, p < .001). However, better-ear SRT did not moderate this relationship (p = .659).
Conclusion: In this UK Biobank sample, poorer speech-in-noise performance was associated with lower cognitive performance, but objectively measured physical activity did not moderate this association. Greater levels of objective physical activity were associated with lower social isolation, and this association was not influenced by hearing ability. These findings suggest that physical activity may be relevant to social isolation outcomes in later life, but the present cross-sectional behavioural data do not support physical activity as a moderator of the association between speech-in-noise hearing ability and cognitive performance.

articles.title: Investigating the Neurobiology of Minority Stress-related Moral Injury with fMRI
articles.authors: Andrew Nicholson; Emma Lynn; Ally H. Villeneuve; Victoria Klimkowski; Magdalena Siegel; Jillian Horning; Taylor Hatchard; Sandhya Narikuzhy; Mina Pichtikova; Ruth Lanius
articles.abstract:
Background
Sexual and gender minorities (SGMs) face unique, chronic stressors and trauma connected to their stigmatized identities, contributing to disproportionately high rates of mental health conditions. Emerging research suggests that these identity-based minority stressors may function as morally injurious events. Here, we aimed to identify the neural correlates of SGM-based moral injury to better understand the biological processes associated with minority stress exposure and downstream trauma-related symptoms that can burden SGM communities.
 
Methods
Our sample included n=39 SGM participants with diverse racial and ethnic identities. We collected functional magnetic resonance imaging data while participants recalled two autobiographical memories via personalized scripts – one morally injurious event related to their SGM identity and one neutral event. Here, we conducted paired sample t-tests exploring neural activation patterns during moral injury memory recall as compared to neutral memory recall [p-family wise error (FWE)-corrected < .05]. Participants completed a battery of questionnaires assessing minority stress, trauma exposure, and trauma-related symptoms, whereby linear regression analyses were conducted to explore associations with neural activation data. 
 
Results
We found increased activation in the left anterior and right posterior insula (i.e., nodes of the salience network) during moral injury as compared to neutral memory recall. Additionally, we uncovered a negative correlation between minority stress exposure and activity within the ventromedial prefrontal cortex (i.e., a major default mode network hub) during moral injury as compared to neutral memory recall. Minority stress exposure was found to be significantly associated with trauma symptom severity. 
 
Conclusions
Our findings of provide preliminary evidence linking identity-based moral injury to disruptions in large-scale brain networks implicated in threat detection, self-referential processing, and emotion. Importantly, this work highlights potential neural targets for trauma-informed interventions aimed at addressing moral injury-related symptoms that disproportionately affect SGM communities.

articles.title: Vision and body representation: Insights from blindness
articles.authors: Dominika Radziun; Luke E. Miller
articles.abstract: Body representations arise from the integration of multiple sensory signals that provide information about the body’s size, posture, and internal states. Vision often plays a dominant role, calibrating and aligning signals from touch, proprioception, and interoception. Yet, individuals born without sight still construct coherent and functional body representations, suggesting that the role of vision in building these representations may be more flexible than previously thought. Here, we synthesize recent behavioral and neuroimaging findings on body representations in blind individuals. We argue that blindness offers a powerful case study in how body representations can emerge through non-visual pathways, revealing the brain’s capacity to flexibly reorganize the sensory inputs supporting its internal models of the body. In doing so, we highlight the broader relevance of visual loss for understanding the plastic and multisensory nature of body representation.

articles.title: Passive Digital Phenotyping for Identifying Dynamic Symptom Patterns: Toward Precision Monitoring in Psychiatry
articles.authors: Rony Kapel Lev-ari; Christian A. Webb; Doron Amsalem; Annika C. Sweetland; Yuval Neria; Milton Wainberg
articles.abstract:
Abstract:
Background:
Mental health symptoms fluctuate over short timeframes, yet clinical assessment typically relies on infrequent self-report, limiting the ability to capture dynamic symptom patterns. Passive digital phenotyping enables continuous, low-burden monitoring of behavioral signals associated with mental health, but the clinical meaning of short-term passive symptom trajectories remains poorly understood. Precision psychiatry calls for approaches that enable individualized characterization of symptom trajectories to inform stratified and responsive treatment.
Methods:
Anonymized passive digital phenotyping data from 13,098 adults were analyzed using a smartphone application that generated daily Mental Health Similarity Scores (MHSS) for depression, anxiety, stress, and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) across seven consecutive days, approximating the interval between routine weekly clinical assessments, using validated machine-learning models anchored to standard clinical questionnaires. Latent class growth analyses identified short-term trajectories, and bivariate models examined depression-anxiety co-fluctuation and stratification by depression burden.
Results:
Depression and anxiety demonstrated heterogeneous short-term trajectories, including stable low, stable high and fluctuating patterns, suggesting distinct short-term symptom dynamics. In contrast, stress and ADHD were largely stable over time. Bivariate analyses identified four synchronized depression-anxiety trajectory classes, ranging from stable low to fluctuating co-occurring profiles. Higher depression was associated with persistently elevated and less variable anxiety patterns.
Conclusions:
Passive digital phenotyping offers a scalable, low-burden approach for continuous symptom monitoring, enabling identification of dynamic risk and resilience profiles at the individual level. Trajectory-based digital phenotypes may support precision psychiatry by informing patient stratification, early detection of symptom change, and more adaptive and personalized approaches to monitoring and intervention.

Key Words: Passive digital phenotyping; Mental health; Precision Psychiatry

articles.title: An Inductive Reasoning Model of Temporal Self-Perception
articles.authors: Johannes Ullrich; David Joachim Grüning; Joachim Krueger
articles.abstract: How do people perceive their selves across time? To shed light on the question of how continuity and growth relate to each other, we extend the inductive reasoning model (IRM; Krueger et al., 2024-a, 2024-b) from social perception to temporal self-perception. Based on the robust empirical patterns showing that people perceive their present selves to be (a) positive and (b) more similar to their future than to their past selves, the IRM makes precise predictions about how much the positivity of the future self will exceed the positivity of the past self (i.e., subjective growth). We find support for the IRM in (re-)analyses of six datasets from Western samples (total N = 8,679). Moreover, we find evidence for additional self-enhancement in that subjective growth is greater than predicted; people enhance their future self, but do not diminish the positivity of their past self. Lastly, we discuss opportunities for future research, such as the use of individual differences in model parameters as correlates of mental health, aging, or culture.

articles.title: Beyond group comparisons: Profiling sentence comprehension in Spanish-speaking children with hearing loss and with typical hearing
articles.authors: Analí Taboh; Diego Shalom; Carolina Gattei
articles.abstract: This study investigates comprehension of spoken sentences with varying morphosyntactic complexity in Spanish-speaking children with prelingual hearing loss (CHL) and children with typical hearing (CTH) matched on auditory experience. We compare comprehension abilities between the groups and explore the development of comprehension strategies by analyzing theoretically defined comprehension profiles across sentence types. Participants with three to 11 years of auditory experience completed a tablet-based sentence-picture matching task. CHL predominantly relied on an agent-first strategy, showing accurate comprehension of simple subject-verb-object sentences and subject relatives, but persistent difficulties with object topicalization, passives, and object relatives. CTH showed progress along the age range examined, with older children usually achieving comprehension of all structures except object relatives. Data-driven k-means clustering supported the theoretical profiles. These findings highlight distinct comprehension strategies and developmental trajectories in later childhood, demonstrating persistent morphosyntactic challenges in CHL and providing a framework for interpreting individual differences in sentence processing.

articles.title: Attitudes about Active Shooter Drills and School Safety among  Adolescents and Young Adults in the United States
articles.authors: Brian M. Hicks; Sarah Stilwell; Dave Kobel; Justin E. Heinze
articles.abstract: Understanding student attitudes toward emergency preparedness drills (“drills”) in response to an active shooter is critical to developing best practices and guidance for schools implementing them. We utilized a national sample of middle and high school students and young adults (N = 1,901) to examine perceptions of school actions when conducting drills including notifications before drills, debriefing, and simulated gunfire. Respondents broadly agreed that drills do not create unnecessary anxiety and should continue to be implemented. Nearly half of respondents reported feeling unprepared in the event of an active shooter, indicating a need to improve drill procedures and training. Debriefing following drills was associated with less drill-related anxiety, feeling more prepared, and taking drills seriously. Notifying before drills and simulating gunshots did not affect responses, especially after controlling for debriefing. Results support more focus on quality debriefing following active shooter drills and that debriefs can have operational and socio-emotional advantages.

articles.title: Afloat or Adrift: A Longitudinal Study of Latent Personality Profiles and Future-of-Work Skills Across Midlife
articles.authors: Matthew J Monnot
articles.abstract: A pressing question during the current artificial intelligence (AI)-driven economic transformation is whether workers will develop and retain AI-related workforce skills. Those skills rest on psychological resources, yet little longitudinal evidence tracks whether workers recover or disengage when those resources are strained. In a secondary analysis of the Midlife in the United States (MIDUS) national panel (N = 7,108; approximately 20 years) and independent Refresher (N = 3,577), latent personality profiles were enumerated from Big Five and Agency indicators. A joint latent Markov model of profile transitions was estimated. Study 1 addressed research questions on latent profile structure, replication, and incremental validity. Study 2 tested six hypotheses on transition structure, transition pathways, skill-criterion change, and self-determination theory predictors of transition direction. Four profiles were supported: Resilient (36.4%), Distressed (29.5%), Reserved (29.0%), and Antagonistic (5.1%). Resilient members reported highest psychosocial skills; Antagonistic members reported highest income, prestige, and scored highest on analytic performance. Profile membership showed no incremental predictive validity beyond continuous traits. Distressed profile membership declined from 29.5% to 7.2% across two decades via recovery (movement to Resilient) and disengagement (movement to Reserved) pathways. Leaving the Distressed profile was associated with lower health-related lost productive time (recovered movers -$3,049 per worker-year, 95% CI [-$5,038, -$1,060]). Purpose predicted recovery- versus disengagement-oriented transition (OR = 1.23 per SD, 95% CI [1.01, 1.50]). Event-sampled diary data (N = 2,314) corroborated profile interpretation. Implications for sustaining workforce skills during AI-era economic transition are discussed.

articles.title: Biased Motive Inferences of Online Outrage Undermine Cross-Partisan Conversations
articles.authors: Chen-Wei Yu; William J. Brady
articles.abstract: Moral outrage spreads widely in online political discourse, but how do people understand others’ outrage expressions? Across three studies (N = 1,855), including behavioral experiments and a field study, we discovered that partisan-biased motive inferences underlie the divergent effects of online outrage expression: While people typically inferred that their in-partisans’ motives for expressing outrage were to raise awareness or inspire action, they tended to infer their political opponents’ motives were to shame or troll. These motive inferences were linked to greater political sectarianism and lower willingness to have a conversation about politics with the outrage expressor. In a fourth study (N = 720), we developed an intervention that changed people’s motive inferences, which improved willingness to have a conversation about politics. These findings highlight the role of motive inferences in shaping contemporary online political discourse filled with strong emotions, and suggest key levers to foster civil interactions among cross-partisans.

articles.title: Emotion regulation strategies produce distinct downstream effects on emotional memory
articles.authors: Jacob Buergler; Kayla Clark; Beatriz M Brandao; Madelyn Castro; Bryan Denny; Stephanie L Leal
articles.abstract: While stressful life events are inevitable, we can apply emotion regulation (ER) strategies to alter how these events impact our cognition and well-being. Although cognitive reappraisal strategies have been shown to effectively modulate emotion, their downstream impacts on memory are less clear. Here, we investigated how distancing and reinterpretation applied to negative images and immersion applied to positive images during memory encoding impact self-reported emotion and subsequent memory. We utilized a memory task that measures general and detailed memory to determine whether ER differentially impacts distinct aspects of memory. Participants were instructed to engage in distancing and immersion or reinterpretation and immersion during memory encoding of emotional images. A third group of participants received no instruction to regulate their emotions and viewed the images as they normally would. As expected, distancing and reinterpretation reduced negative affect toward negative images, whereas immersion increased positive affect toward positive images. Across ER groups, images encoded during ER-cued trials were generally better remembered than images viewed passively, with enhanced performance observed for both general and detailed memory. However, detailed memory showed additional strategy- and valence-dependent effects. Immersion was associated with enhanced detailed memory for positive images, distancing was associated with reduced detailed memory for negative images, and reinterpretation did not significantly alter detailed memory for negative images. These findings suggest that engaging ER during encoding may broadly enhance subsequent memory, while specific strategies selectively shape the fidelity of emotional memories, highlighting the importance of considering downstream cognitive consequences when selecting strategies to promote emotional well-being.

articles.title: Default nudges modulate the temporal profile of pupil-linked arousal during decision-making under cognitive load
articles.authors: Mercede Erfanian; Teye; Marco Heimann; Luc Meunier; Jean-Francois Gajewski
articles.abstract: The mechanisms by which default nudges influence complex decision-making under cognitive load remain poorly understood. Although defaults can shape choice behaviour, behavioural measures alone cannot reveal how they affect covert cognitive processes. We tested whether default nudges reduce task-evoked pupil responses or instead alter their temporal profile during complex decision-making. An online study (N = 89) first behaviourally validated five levels of digit-span working-memory load for use in the subsequent laboratory experiment. In the laboratory study (N = 56), participants completed complex decision task embedded within the validated working-memory paradigm while pupil diameter was recorded. Cognitive load produced the expected parametric increase in encoding-locked pupil responses, confirming the sensitivity of the manipulation to working-memory demands. Behaviourally, default nudges did not significantly influence decision accuracy, default-consistent responding, decision response time, recall accuracy, or recall response time. Pupil responses revealed a different pattern. During the decision interval, participants exposed to a nudge showed more pronounced decision-locked pupil responses than those without, particularly when the nudge was accepted. During recall, this pattern reversed, with the No Nudge group exhibiting larger recall-locked pupil responses than the Nudge group. These phase-dependent effects indicate that default presentation altered the temporal profile of pupil-linked arousal across the task rather than producing a uniform reduction in task-evoked pupil responses. The findings suggest that nudges, and nudge acceptance in particular, is not associated with reduced pupil responses but may involve active evaluation of a preselected response (nudge) before commitment, challenging strong effort-saving accounts of default nudges during complex decision-making.

articles.title: What have we learned about human reasoning from large reasoning models?   Response to de Varda et al.
articles.authors: Jeffrey S Bowers; Ivan Vankov; Federico G Adolfi; Rachel Flood Heaton; Guillermo Puebla
articles.abstract: de Varda et al (2025) reported that human response times and the number of tokens generated by a range of large reasoning models (LRMs) are correlated across 7 different tasks. The authors took the findings to reflect a “strong alignment” between reasoning effort in LRMs and humans.  In response to a critique of Vankov et al. (2026), de Varda et al (2026a) carried out a new series of simulation studies taken to support their original claims and to clarify what they mean by strong alignment.  Here we reinterpret their findings and conclude that their findings have no implications for human reasoning.  We also take their clarification of strong alignment as a “motte and bailey” argument that is common in NeuroAI.

articles.title: Developing a psychological test battery to measure cognition in daily life
articles.authors: Andrew J. Aschenbrenner; Muchen Xi; Jeremy Cohn; Derek Alexander Simon; Joshua James Jackson
articles.abstract: Cognition is not a static process but is subject to substantial and meaningful variation within individuals over time. This has led to an increase in studies that aim to describe cognition in daily life by sampling participants repeatedly and remotely. Such studies, which we call high-frequency cognitive assessment or HFCA, tend to use a limited number of brief cognitive tests. This focus on a small number of tests leaves open questions concerning the psychometric characteristics of a wide array of cognitive tasks useful for HFCA that can guide researchers on appropriate task selection. We developed the Cognitive Variability Battery (CVB) a series of 9 cognitive tests clustered into three distinct cognitive domains, attentional control, processing speed, and episodic memory. CVB was administered to participants 3 times per day for 3 weeks. Cognitive tests were rotated to reduce the length of any single testing session. Each test was administered up to 60 times. We provide detailed descriptions of the performance of each task including variability, skew, and reliability statistics using intraclass correlations. We examine the sensitivity of each test to several contextual factors including stress, affect and social interactions. Finally, we provide power analyses on each cognitive test to determine how many assessments and participants are needed to detect effects of interest. These analyses will be essential to anyone seeking to implement HFCA testing in their own research programs by providing guidance on which cognitive tests to select and how many participants and observations may be needed.

articles.title: Predictors of Problematic Binge Watching: The moderating role of sensation seeking and the mediating role of mental health
articles.authors: Zaheer Hussain; Katie Alberici; Caroline A Harvey
articles.abstract: Binge watching (BW) TV series is now a popular phenomenon. However, there are legitimate concerns about BW and its similarities to other problematic online behaviours. Understanding how a healthy behaviour may transition to becoming problematic requires further investigation. The present study examined the predictors of problematic binge watching (PBW); hypothesising that impulsivity, anxiety, watching engagement, sensation seeking, and low levels of mental health would be associated with PBW. The moderating effect of sensation seeking in the relationship between watching engagement and PBW, and the mediating effect of mental health in the relationship between anxiety and PBW was also assessed. In total, 1,257 participants (mean age = 33.8 years, SD = 10.7) completed an online survey consisting of a battery of scales. Results revealed that number of months watching TV series, watching engagement, anxiety, impulsivity, and sensation seeking significantly predicted PBW with a large effect size. The interaction between watching engagement and sensation seeking was statistically significant, indicating sensation seeking significantly moderated the relationship between watching engagement and PBW. Furthermore, the relationship between anxiety and PBW was partially mediated by mental health. The findings showed support for direct and indirect pathways through which individuals traits shape PBW, future research is discussed.

articles.title: Checklist of Metacognitive Aspects of Transferable Skills (CheckMATS): A new tool for educational research and practice
articles.authors: Anna Tychmanowicz; Magdalena Olempska-Wysocka; Tomasz Przybyla; Aneta Wojciechowska; Joanna Doroszuk; Karina Leksy; Gregory Kroliczak; Michal Klichowski
articles.abstract: Metacognitive aspects of transferable skills—the capacity to regulate one's cognitive processes to enable skill application across diverse contexts—are critical for lifelong learning and occupational adaptability. Yet, no validated tool for their assessment has existed. Here we present the Checklist of Metacognitive Aspects of Transferable Skills (CheckMATS). It is an exceptionally easy-to-use instrument available in four age-adjusted versions spanning all educational stages, from early childhood through adulthood. A study conducted in a sample of 1,243 participants drawn from 31 educational institutions—including preschools, primary schools, general secondary schools, secondary technical schools, and vocational schools—confirmed satisfactory psychometric properties of the proposed tool. All CheckMATS versions demonstrate acceptable to good internal consistency (KR-20 between 0.70 and 0.88). Importantly, the metacognitive aspects of transferable skills they assess correlate with developmentally relevant psychological constructs, including interoception, theory of mind, metacognitive awareness, and selected aspects of metacognitive beliefs, supporting theoretical validity. These findings establish CheckMATS as a practical, psychometrically sound tool that addresses a longstanding gap in educational assessment, with potential applications ranging from classroom monitoring of individual development to scientific research. In the spirit of open science, all CheckMATS versions are made freely available alongside this article in editable format, enabling their use as paper-and-pencil instruments or implementation in electronic forms.

articles.title: A Fresh Start? A Scoping Review of Health Behavior Change around the New Year
articles.authors: Dylan Keith Richards; Kaitlin Woolley; Adam Kent Fetterman; Nina Caitlin Christie; Katie Witkiewitz
articles.abstract: Background: Modifiable health behaviors are major contributors to death and disability. Each January, millions of people attempt to change these behaviors through New Year’s resolutions, providing an exceptional opportunity to study and promote health behavior change. Purpose: We conducted a scoping review to characterize the literature on the new year as a temporal landmark for health behavior change and identify gaps to guide future research. Methods: Following PRISMA-ScR guidelines, we searched PsycINFO, PubMed, and Web of Science for peer-reviewed studies examining New Year’s resolutions or changes in health-related motivation, engagement, and behavior surrounding the new year. Study characteristics, methods, health behaviors, outcomes, and key findings were extracted and synthesized narratively. Results: Twenty-five articles representing 27 independent studies met the inclusion criteria. Studies addressed three broad questions: whether the new year increases motivation and initial engagement with health behavior change (k = 10), whether individuals successfully maintain New Year’s resolutions over time (k = 13), and whether initiating health behavior change around the new year improves outcomes (k = 4). Evidence was strongest that the new year is associated with increased motivation and initial engagement in health behavior change attempts. Evidence regarding long-term maintenance and improved outcomes was promising but limited by methodological heterogeneity, and few studies directly assessed changes in health behaviors. Conclusions: The new year may represent an important temporal landmark for health behavior change. Future studies using validated health outcomes are needed to determine whether increased motivation during this time translates into sustained behavior change.

articles.title: A cross-generational investigation of physical health, mental health, and lifestyle during the COVID-19 pandemic in The Netherlands: results from network analyses
articles.authors: Kirsten van Hooijdonk; Sasja Danieke Noach; Roy Otten; Jacqueline Vink
articles.abstract: The coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID 19) pandemic substantially affected daily life and health. This preregistered study used nationally representative data from three Dutch Corona Public Health Monitors to conceptualise health during the pandemic as a system of mutually reinforcing components across four generations (166,252 youth, 69,750 young adults, 185,443 adults, and 171,076 elderly individuals). First, per generation, sample characteristics were compared between low- and high-pandemic-impact groups, using chi-square tests (Aim 1). Second, cross-sectional network analyses (Mixed Graphical Models) were used to examine how physical health, mental health, and lifestyle were interrelated within all age and impact groups (Aim 2). Finally, all networks were compared to distinguish shared and age-/impact-specific constellations of key health factors (Aim 3). Across generations, experiencing financial difficulties was identified as a key factor increasing the likelihood of belonging to the high-impact group (Aim 1). In all networks (Aim 2), perceived general health emerged as one of the most central nodes, with strong connections to mental health and physical activity. In addition, unique key health factors were identified in all networks, highlighting the distinctiveness of each network per generation and pandemic-impact group (Aim 3). Together, these analyses generate actionable insights for national, regional, and local policymakers by providing a nuanced understanding of how pandemic-related stress is embedded in health networks across the life course.
