articles.title: Parental Digital Tracking of Adolescents’ School Performance, Location, and Finances: Widespread, Often Accepted, and Linked to Overprotection
articles.authors: Savannah Boele; Anne Bülow; Loes Keijsers
articles.abstract: Introduction. Digital tracking tools are now at parents’ fingertips, raising concerns about infringement on adolescents’ autonomy, privacy, and well-being. Despite growing concerns about parental digital surveillance, empirical research beyond location tracking remains limited. This study examined parental digital tracking across three key domains: school performance, location, and finances. Methods. This is a multi-informant, cross-sectional survey study (2024) including 525 Dutch parent–adolescent dyads (adolescents: Mage=14.1, range=11-18; 53% female; parents: Mage=46.7, 81% mothers). A second sample (N = 175 dyads; 2019) tested replication and changes over time. Results. In 2024, nearly all parents (99.6%) tracked at least one domain. Most adolescents accepted tracking, though location tracking was accepted less. Younger, less educated parents, and mothers tracked more frequently, particularly school performance. Adolescents following a lower secondary educational track were tracked more frequently. Younger adolescents and boys experienced more frequent school tracking, whereas older adolescents were tracked more frequently in location. Digital tracking was unrelated to adolescent well-being (e.g., anxiety symptoms) but positively associated with parental control- and fear-related factors (e.g., overprotection, dangerous worldviews). School and location tracking increased over the past five years, as did adolescents’ acceptance of tracking. Conclusions. Parental digital tracking appears a common tool for many parents today and its frequent use may reflect parental insecurities, with no clear link to adolescent maladjustment. Longitudinal research is needed to examine whether digital tracking reassures parents or reinforces fears, which might undermine parents’ - and potentially also adolescents’ - well-being.

articles.title: The Microsystem Matters: Using machine learning to identify moderators of longitudinal  parenting effects on adolescent internalizing problems
articles.authors: Savannah Boele; Stefanos Mastrotheodoros; Caspar J. Van Lissa
articles.abstract:
Background: Despite decades of research on parenting, it remains unclear why the same 
practices benefit some adolescents but not others. Prior research on moderators that could explain 
heterogeneous parenting effects has typically examined just one or a few potential factors and 
yielded mixed findings. The present study cast a wider net, evaluating 129 potential moderators 
to identify the most important determinants of heterogeneity in within-family parenting effects on 
adolescents’ internalizing problems. Methods: Participants were 7,928 adolescents and their 
7,840 mothers and 6,777 fathers enrolled in the Longitudinal Study of Australian Children 
(LSAC). Parents reported on parenting (warmth, inductive reasoning, low angry parenting) and 
adolescents reported on internalizing problems for four biannual waves (age 10-16). Time-lagged 
within-family parenting effects were estimated using Random-Intercept Cross-Lagged Panel 
Models, and SEM-forests were used to evaluate 129 time-invariant moderators spanning multiple 
levels of the bioecological model. Results: On average, all parenting practices negatively 
predicted internalizing problems, with substantial heterogeneity across families. The effect of 
maternal warmth was most heterogeneous, being protective in some families and harmful in 
others. The most influential moderators across all practices were family microsystem 
characteristics, in particular father involvement and parental life difficulties. Despite being an 
important moderator, father involvement’s marginal moderating effects were approximately flat, 
suggesting that it might interact with other family characteristics. Parental life difficulties 
diminished protective parenting effects. Conclusions: Macro-timescale parenting effects on 
adolescent internalizing problems are heterogeneous across families, and this heterogeneity 
depends primarily on the family microsystem rather than on individual adolescent characteristics. 
These findings suggest that one-size-fits-all approaches to parenting research and intervention are 
insufficient, and call for greater attention to the family context.

articles.title: Awareness is Predictably Lossy
articles.authors: Ariel berlinger; Ariel Goldstein; Baruch Eitam
articles.abstract: When something is plainly in view, are we always aware of seeing it, and is awareness always beneficial? We tested whether a clearly visible but task-irrelevant feature can fail to become reportable while still guiding behavior. Across four experiments (N = 584), participants viewed meaningful two-part objects under prolonged, unmasked exposure, with only one-part task-relevant. When unexpectedly asked to report the irrelevant part, participants performed at chance; yet the same feature reliably guided choices in a perceptual comparison task (55% and 60% correct; chance = 33%). The advantage belonged to the least aware: participants who reported noticing no change outperformed those who did, an inverse relationship confirmed in a large preregistered replication. Awareness is not simply stronger perception, but a selective transformation of what we see.

articles.title: Dissociating Eye and Mouth Contributions to Dynamic Face Processing with Frequency Tagging
articles.authors: Yasemin Gunindi; Çiçek Güney; Huseyin Ozkan; Nihan Alp
articles.abstract: Dynamic face perception depends on how local information from moving face parts is used within the broader configuration of the face. The present study used a temporal-direction discrimination task to examine the part-based neural contributions of the eyes and mouth during dynamic face processing. Across two experiments, Turkish and non-Turkish speakers judged whether muted videos of neutral faces articulating Turkish speech were presented forward or backward in time, while the eye and mouth regions were independently frequency-tagged in the EEG. Face orientation and blink presence were manipulated to assess how canonical face configuration and local dynamic cues shape part-based responses. Behaviorally, participants discriminated temporal direction above chance, with higher sensitivity for upright faces and with-blink face videos. Turkish speakers showed higher sensitivity than non-Turkish speakers specifically for upright faces, suggesting that language familiarity facilitated behavioral judgments when speech-related facial information was available in its canonical configuration. In the EEG, frequency-tagged responses were stronger for the mouth than for the eye, possibly reflecting the more sustained visual input generated by continuous articulatory mouth movements compared with the more transient motion in the eye region. Blink presence selectively enhanced eye-related responses, and face orientation modulated the differentiation between eye- and mouth-related responses. However, temporal direction did not produce a robust overall difference in frequency-tagged response strength, and language group did not modulate the tagged responses. Overall, the findings suggest that temporal-direction discrimination relies on how eye- and mouth-related cues are used within the face configuration, while frequency-tagged EEG responses reveal condition-dependent differences in the visual encoding of these dynamic face parts.

articles.title: Implementing Dimensional and Transdiagnostic Mental Health Assessment in Psycho-Oncology: Validation of the HiTOP Brief Report (HiTOP-BR) in Cancer Survivors
articles.authors: Jai Carmichael; Annika Hegde; Martin Sellbom; Nicolas Hart; Darren Haywood
articles.abstract: Assessment of psychopathology among cancer survivors often relies on measures of generalized psychological distress or unstructured approaches, limiting the comprehensive assessment of mental health difficulties. Contemporary dimensional and transdiagnostic frameworks, such as the Hierarchical Taxonomy of Psychopathology (HiTOP), offer a framework for more comprehensive structure and assessment. We evaluated the psychometric properties of the 45-item HiTOP Brief Report (HiTOP-BR) in cancer survivors. Participants were 728 adults with a current (n = 155) or past (n = 573) cancer diagnosis who were recruited and completed the HiTOP-BR online alongside other cancer-specific measures. All primary and secondary scales demonstrated good internal consistency (αs and ωs > .80). Relative to general community data, participants with current cancer showed elevations across the Somatoform, Internalizing, Thought Disorder, Antagonism, and p-Factor dimensions and scored higher than participants with past cancer across all dimensions except Detachment. Among participants with past cancer, elevations relative to general community data were confined to the Somatoform spectrum. Confirmatory factor analysis broadly supported the proposed six-spectra structure, with all items loading meaningfully on their intended factors. A bifactor model identified a strong general psychopathology factor (ωH = .84), although substantial variance remained attributable to the specific spectra (ECV = .56). Higher HiTOP-BR scores were associated with poorer physical functioning and greater fear of cancer progression and recurrence. The HiTOP-BR appears to be a reliable and valid tool for assessing psychopathology dimensions that may be elevated among cancer survivors and facilitating implementation of dimensional and transdiagnostic approaches within psycho-oncology.

articles.title: A Single-Arm Longitudinal Pilot Study of Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu as a Mental Health Intervention for Combat Veterans with Military-Connected Disabilities
articles.authors: Jack Ryan Kaufman; Wyatt R. Evans; Robert W. Haley; C. Munro Cullum
articles.abstract: Combat veterans experience increased incidences of depression, anxiety, and PTSD, along with challenges when adjusting to life post-discharge, but have been under-served using traditional mental health treatments. Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu has emerged as potentially therapeutic for combat veterans, although empirical support is lacking. A single-arm pre-post pilot study was used to evaluate seven psychosocial outcomes among participants from the We Defy Foundation program (n = 40; 87.5% male; Mage = 41.1, SD = 5.8). The primary outcomes measured were post-traumatic stress severity (PTSD Checklist for DSM-5; PCL-5), depression (Patient Health Questionnaire-9; PHQ-9), anxiety (Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7; GAD-7), and Military-Civilian Transition Quality (M2CQ). Secondary outcomes included Self-Efficacy (General Self-Efficacy Scale; GSE), Functional Disability (World Health Organization Disability Assessment Schedule; WHODAS 2.0), and Life Satisfaction (Satisfaction with Life Scale; SWLS). Assessments were completed at baseline (T0), 3 months (T3; n = 34), and 6 months (T6; n = 23, final). Results revealed significant improvements in the four primary outcomes, which demonstrated high symptom severity scores at baseline, at both T3 (Cohen’s dz = .52-.63) and T6 (dz = .84-1.04) after applying the Benjamini-Hochberg False Discovery Rate (FDR) correction. Two of the three secondary outcomes achieved statistical significance at T3 (GSE and SWLS) and WHODAS became statistically significant at T6. These preliminary findings indicate BJJ participation resulted in positive accumulative mental health improvements for this veteran population and provides a promising therapeutic target for future studies.

articles.title: Before and beyond the pandemic: Dynamics of illegal marine wildlife trade in Southern China amidst policy shifts and enforcement efforts
articles.authors: Wuyin Lin; KuoRayMao; Xinyin Zhao
articles.abstract: This study examines the illegal marine wildlife trade in Southern China, focusing on sea turtles, giant clams, and corals, to assess enforcement challenges, market dynamics, and consumer behaviors. Adopting a multi-method approach, it incorporates a comprehensive policy and regulatory review spanning 1979–2022, along with market and consumer surveys conducted before and after the COVID-19 pandemic. Standardized training protocols were used for data collection, including consumer questionnaires and stakeholder interviews with a diverse range of actors. Market surveys reveal a 17.06 % decrease in the number of shops selling marine wildlife products but a 32.72 % increase in items available for sale, suggesting a concentration of trade activity. Consumer data indicate that the majority of potential buyers were aged 23–30 (38.93 %) and 31–45 (24.83 %), with 60 % identifying as female. Stakeholder interviews identify distinct supply chain nodes facilitating illegal trade across the region. Despite policy reforms and intensified enforcement at the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic, the study finds that marine species remain vulnerable due to fragmented regulations and inconsistent enforcement across jurisdictions. Sellers continue to exploit short-term, top-down enforcement gaps, maintaining illicit trade flows and meeting persistent consumer demand. The findings underscore the resilience of illegal trade networks and the inadequacy of reactive enforcement strategies. A multi-stakeholder approach—grounded in inter-agency coordination and civic engagement—is essential. Without sustained, community-driven enforcement mechanisms, policy efforts will remain ineffective, exacerbating illegal trade and accelerating biodiversity loss in China and the wider Global South.

articles.title: 'Racism is Stronger than Both of Our Papers': Formerly Undocumented Latino Immigrants' Emergent Shared Racial Status with Black Americans
articles.authors: Luis Edward Tenorio
articles.abstract:
Extant research presumes the relations between Latino immigrants and Black Americans to be competitive
and conflictual, with Latino immigrants’ undocumented status contributing to such intergroup dynamics.
However, might the transition from undocumented to lawful permanent resident (LPR) status change Latino
immigrants’ attitudes towards, and perceptions of, Black Americans? If so, how? Drawing on interviews
and observations with currently and formerly undocumented Latino immigrants across the Los Angeles and
Atlanta metropolitan areas, I find obtaining LPR status positively shifts Latino immigrants’ reported
attitudes towards, and perceptions of, Black Americans. Informed by racial status theory, I outline this
finding as a function of two post-legalization mechanisms: changes in intergroup contact and a shared sense
of discrimination. By enabling formerly undocumented respondents to envision a permanent life for
themselves in the United States and enhancing their access and comfort with institutional resources (e.g.,
employment authorization; banking accounts) LPR status facilitated expanded spatial mobility, social
engagement, and entry into new spaces (e.g., workplaces, neighborhoods). This increased contact quality
with Black Americans, allowing for the accumulation of observations and experiences that challenged prior
negative perceptions of Black Americans. Further, as formerly undocumented immigrants increased their
engagement in society with LPR status, so too did their exposure to assumptions/suspicions of being
undocumented and active denial of social or economic recognition by others. Confronting this reality shifted
the primary lens through which they understood their position and experiences in the United States from
legal status to an ethnoracial consciousness. Overall, my findings highlight legalization as a critical
mechanism for ethnoracial consciousness through intergroup perceptions and attitudes.

articles.title: "FROM 'CLOSING DOWN THE DEEP-BORE WELLS' TO THE WANDERING EARTH: A Re-examination of Environmental Governance Legitimacy in China".
articles.authors: KuoRayMao
articles.abstract: The article critically examines the role of environmental law in China's state-capitalist system from a structural Marxist perspective. The author argues that the Chinese environmental regulatory regime, often perceived as arbitrary and chaotic, is not a mere byproduct of a developing legal system but a deliberate strategy to legitimize state authority and control. Through case studies on integrated water resources management and the prevention of husbandry waste pollution, the article illustrates how environmental laws serve as both Repressive State Apparatuses (RSA) and Ideological State Apparatuses (ISA), enforcing social control and shaping public consciousness. The state's top-down enforcement methods, reliance on technocratic solutions, and manipulation of legal and moral ideologies are shown to maintain and obscure the relations of production, reinforcing the state-capitalist model of accumulation. The article also explores how China's cultural products like the film, The Wandering Earth, normalize authoritarian state authority in global environmental governance. The analysis concludes that to fully understand China's environmental governance, one must view it through the lens of state-capitalist accumulation, recognizing the role of environmental law in maintaining authoritarian state-society relations and shaping the broader political-economic landscape.

articles.title: Gender Disparities in International Research Collaboration: Study of 25,000 University Professors
articles.authors: Marek Kwiek; Wojciech Roszka
articles.abstract: In this large-scale research based on bibliometric, biographical and administrative data, we examine how gender disparities in international research collaboration differ by collaboration intensity, academic position, age, and academic discipline. The following are the major findings: (1) While female scientists exhibit a higher rate of general, national, and institutional collaboration, male scientists exhibit a higher rate of international collaboration. (2) An aggregated picture of gender disparities hides a more nuanced cross-disciplinary picture of them. (3) An analysis of international research collaboration at three separate intensity levels (low, medium, and high) reveals that male scientists dominate in international collaboration at each level. However, at each level, there are specific disciplines in which females collaborate internationally more than males. Furthermore (4), gender disparities in international research collaboration are clearly linked with age: they are the lowest and statistically insignificant for young scientists and the highest and statistically significant for the oldest scientists. Finally, we estimate the odds ratios of being involved in international research collaboration using an analytical linear logistic model. The examined sample includes 25,463 internationally visible Polish university professors from 85 universities, grouped into 24 disciplines, and 158,743 Scopus-indexed articles.

articles.title: Are female scientists less inclined to publish alone? The gender solo research gap
articles.authors: Marek Kwiek; Wojciech Roszka
articles.abstract: In solo research, scientists compete individually for prestige, sending clear signals about their research ability, avoiding problems in credit allocation, and reducing conflicts about authorship. We examine to what extent male and female scientists differ in their use of solo publishing across various dimensions. This research is the first to comprehensively study the “gender solo research gap” among all internationally visible scientists within a whole national higher education system. We examine the gap through mean “individual solo publishing rates” found in “individual publication portfolios” constructed for each Polish university professor. We use the practical significance/statistical significance difference (based on the effect-size r coefficient) and our analyses indicate that while some gender differences are statistically significant, they have no practical significance. Using a partial effects of fractional logistic regression approach, we estimate the probability of conducting solo research. In none of the models does gender explain the variability of the individual solo publishing rate. The strongest predictor of individual solo publishing rate is the average team size, publishing in STEM fields negatively affects the rate, publishing in male-dominated disciplines positively affects it, and the influence of international collaboration is negative. The gender solo research gap in Poland is much weaker than expected: within a more general trend toward team research and international research, gender differences in solo research are much weaker and less relevant than initially assumed. We use our unique biographical, administrative, publication, and citation database (“Polish Science Observatory”) with metadata on all Polish scientists present in Scopus (N = 25,463) and their 158,743 Scopus-indexed articles published in 2009–2018, including 18,900 solo articles.

articles.title: Quantifying attrition in science: a cohort-based, longitudinal study of scientists in 38 OECD countries
articles.authors: Marek Kwiek; Łukasz Szymula
articles.abstract: In this paper, we explore how members of the scientific community leave academic science and how attrition (defined as ceasing to publish) differs across genders, academic disciplines, and over time. Our approach is cohort-based and longitudinal: We track individual male and female scientists over time and quantify the phenomenon traditionally referred to as “leaving science.” Using publication metadata from Scopus—a global bibliometric database of publications and citations—we follow the details of the publishing careers of scientists from 38 OECD countries who started publishing in 2000 (N = 142,776) and 2010 (N = 232,843). Our study is restricted to 16 STEMM disciplines (science, technology, engineering, mathematics, and medicine), and we track the individual scholarly output of the two cohorts until 2022. We use survival analysis to compare attrition of men and women scientists. With more women in science and more women within cohorts, attrition is becoming ever less gendered. In addition to the combined aggregated changes at the level of all STEMM disciplines, widely nuanced changes were found to occur at the discipline level and over time. Attrition in science means different things for men versus women depending on the discipline; moreover, it means different things for scientists from different cohorts entering the scientific workforce. Finally, global bibliometric datasets were tested in the current study, opening new opportunities to explore gender and disciplinary differences in attrition.

articles.title: The European Research Elite.  A Cross-National Study of Highly Productive Academics in 11 Countries
articles.authors: Marek Kwiek
articles.abstract: In this paper, we focus on a rare scholarly theme of highly productive academics, statistically confirming their pivotal role in knowledge production across 11 systems studied. The upper 10 % of highly productive academics in 11 European countries studied (N = 17,211) provide on average almost half of all academic knowledge production. In contrast to dominating bibliometric studies of research productivity, we focus on academic attitudes, behaviors, and perceptions as predictors of becoming research top performers across European systems. Our paper provides a (large-scale and cross-country) corroboration of the systematic inequality in knowledge production, for the first time argued for by Lotka (J Wash Acad Sci 16:317–323, 1929) and de Solla Price (Little science, big science. Columbia University Press, New York, 1963). We corroborate the deep academic inequality in science and explore this segment of the academic profession. The European research elite is a highly homogeneous group of academics whose high research performance is driven by structurally similar factors, mostly individual rather than institutional. Highly productive academics are similar from a cross-national perspective, and they substantially differ intra-nationally from their lower-performing colleagues.

articles.title: Young male and female scientists: A quantitative exploratory study of the changing demographics of the global scientific workforce
articles.authors: Marek Kwiek; Łukasz Szymula
articles.abstract: In this study, the global scientific workforce is explored through large-scale, generational, cross-sectional, and longitudinal approaches. We examine 4.3 million nonoccasional scientists from 38 OECD countries publishing in 1990–2021. Our interest is in the changing distribution of young male and female scientists over time across 16 science, technology, engineering, mathematics, medicine (STEMM) disciplines. We unpack the details of the changing scientific workforce using age groups. Some disciplines are already numerically dominated by women, and the change is fast in some and slow in others. In one-third of disciplines, there are already more youngest female than male scientists. Across all disciplines combined, the majority of women are young women. And more than half of female scientists (55.02%) are located in medicine. The usefulness of global bibliometric data sources in analyzing the scientific workforce along gender, age, discipline, and time is tested. Traditional aggregated data about scientists in general hide a nuanced picture of the changing gender dynamics within and across disciplines and age groups. The limitations of bibliometric data sets are explored, and global studies are compared with national-level studies. The methodological choices and their implications are shown, and new opportunities for how to study scientists globally are discussed.

articles.title: Authoritarian environmentalism and epistemological violence: A Southern green criminology analysis of the 2014 Lanzhou water crisis and the belt and road initiative expansion into the global water sector
articles.authors: KuoRayMao; Zhong Zhao
articles.abstract: This article examines authoritarian states’ roles in commodifying freshwater resources in illiberal societies. The authors argue that collusion between global capitalism and national authoritarian interests has affected the legal structure, regulation enforcement, and institutional practices of public–private partnerships in China’s municipal water systems, resulting in regulatory failures in drinking water provision. The article also explores the implications of China’s state capitalist expansion into the global water utilities market as part of the green Belt and Road Initiative and suggests that this expansion may lead to new patterns of environmental concerns in the Global South. The findings demonstrate that collusion between neoliberal and authoritarian capitalist expansions shapes increasing inequalities and environmental governance standards in the Global South. The authors stress the need to view environmental and public health disasters resulting from water privatization as a transnational crime rather than solely focusing on nation-state regulatory mechanisms that exemplify “metropolitan thinking” in criminology.

articles.title: Verification Costs and the Boundary of the Firm: A Post-Coasean Theory of Organization Under Synthetic Production
articles.authors: Babu George
articles.abstract: Transaction cost economics has long treated information technology as a force that lowers the cost of transacting and therefore shrinks firm boundaries. Generative and agentic systems break the assumption on which that prediction rests. They collapse the cost of producing an artifact without lowering, and in several documented cases while raising, the cost of establishing that the artifact is fit for use. This paper develops the consequences of that wedge. Three results follow. First, as unit production cost approaches zero and per-unit verification cost remains bounded away from zero, verification's share of total activity cost converges to one, so the make-or-buy question ceases to be about production and becomes a question about verification alone. Second, verification cannot be recursively delegated to automated verifiers whose errors are correlated with those of the generator, and residual liability cannot be assigned to agents that hold no assets and no legal personality; recent decisions in Mata v. Avianca and Moffatt v. Air Canada, together with the allocation of duties under Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, place that residual on the deploying firm. Third, the human judgments produced during verification are the scarce, distribution-specific labels required to improve a firm's own models, which makes verification simultaneously a cost and an appropriable asset. Together these mechanisms predict selective reinternalization of high-consequence knowledge work rather than the continued unbundling that the electronic markets hypothesis anticipated. The paper states six falsifiable predictions with proposed operationalizations, and identifies the conditions, principally the availability of cheap machine-checkable success criteria, under which the opposite prediction should hold.

articles.title: ¿Qué sabemos sobre la agricultura familiar en el Perú?: Revisión crítica de evidencia, enfoques temáticos y vacíos para la política pública
articles.authors: Sebastian Iglesias-Osores
articles.abstract: La agricultura familiar es central para comprender la estructura agraria, la seguridad alimentaria y las políticas rurales en el Perú. Este documento revisa críticamente 46 fuentes centradas en el caso peruano desde 2014 y organiza la evidencia mediante síntesis temática. Los hallazgos muestran avances importantes en caracterización, tipologías y estudios territoriales, pero menor acumulación en evaluación de políticas, extensión agraria, financiamiento, juventud rural, digitalización, inserción comercial diferenciada y trayectorias de transformación. Se plantea que la agenda de investigación debe desplazarse desde la pregunta por cuántos agricultores familiares existen y dónde se ubican hacia qué instrumentos funcionan, para qué productores, en qué territorios y bajo qué condiciones.

articles.title: The double marginalization of the very old as societies age and cultural life moves online
articles.authors: Joonhyung Bae
articles.abstract: As societies age and cultural life moves online, the oldest are most exposed to being left behind. Recovery is usually judged by an aggregate silent about who actually returned, and a widening gap seen in one survey is rarely tested elsewhere. We ask not whether cultural participation recovered after the pandemic but for whom, reading only public attendance-by-age tables for Seoul and five other high-income settings. Across them the oldest sit lowest on both the in-person and the digital channel at once, a double marginalization that going online does not offset: from the published margins alone, nearly one in five of the oldest reach neither channel, a share that is zero for every younger band. Whether recovery widened the young-old gap is local: it widened in Seoul yet reversed, narrowing, in Korea's national survey over the same window. The oldest's disadvantage in level is general; the widening is not.

articles.title: Genetic Mirroring in Adoptees: Toward a Formal Construct Definition, Nomological Network, and Operationalization Framework
articles.authors: Giulia Suzzi
articles.abstract: Genetic mirroring, the developmentally recurring need to perceive reflected biological similarity in genetically related others, has gained clinical salience as an explanatory framework for the identity experiences of adoptees and donor-conceived individuals. Despite this, the construct lacks the theoretical architecture required for empirical investigation: a precise definition, differentiation from adjacent constructs, and a plausible operationalization pathway. The present paper addresses that gap through four coordinated contributions. First, a formal construct definition is proposed, encompassing three theoretically distinct dimensions: biological salience, embodied discontinuity, and mirroring responsiveness. Second, the construct is situated within a nomological network specifying its hypothesized relationships with established psychological variables, including identity exploration, narrative identity coherence, attachment security, genealogical bewilderment, and physical self-concept. Third, a theoretical case is made for incremental validity over existing frameworks: genetic mirroring is proposed to capture variance in adoptee psychological functioning that neither attachment theory nor narrative identity frameworks can fully account for. Fourth, a preliminary scale structure is proposed as proof of concept. The paper's aim is to transform a clinically emergent construct into a formally theorizable and measurable entity, enabling the empirical program necessary to evaluate its scientific and practical significance.

articles.title: Hidden Labor, Hidden Harm: Gendered Trauma and the Paradox of Double Exposure in Federal Probation
articles.authors: Sandra L. Trappen; Ethan Michael Galley; Cristina Figueroa; Bobur Rakhmatullaev
articles.abstract: This U.S.-based study examines how hierarchical structures organize the emotional and relational labor of federal probation officers, shaping the institutional conditions under which justice work occurs. Drawing on a national survey of 423 officers and in-depth interviews with 30 participants, we show how expectations of composure, distributions of relational work, and organizational norms that discourage strain disclosure create patterned vulnerabilities across the workforce. Officers in frontline roles, particularly women officers of color, report heightened demands and scrutiny, revealing how institutional cultures distribute emotional labor and constrain expressions of strain. Qualitative accounts illuminate the paradox of double exposure: officers are both survivors of trauma and practitioners managing others’ trauma within environments that reward stoicism and limit vulnerability. Strain emerges as the operational expression of structurally produced trauma, underscoring that trauma-informed justice must begin with the workforce.

articles.title: MACROECONOMIC RELATIONSHIP OF REMITTANCE INFLOW AND OUTFLOW IN NEPAL: EMPIRICAL EVIDENCE USING ARDL AND XG BOOST
articles.authors: Arjun Gurung
articles.abstract:
Remittance has become one of the main sources of foreign income and an
important part of the Nepalese economy. It plays a significant role in reducing poverty,
increasing household income, and maintaining foreign exchange reserves. The study
entitled “MACROECONOMIC RELATIONSHIP OF REMITTANCE INFLOW AND
OUTFLOW IN NEPAL EMPIRICAL EVIDENCE USING ARDL AND XG BOOST”
has been carried out to examine the relationship of selected macroeconomic variables
with remittance inflow and outflow.
The main objective of this study is to examine the relationship of
macroeconomic indicators real GDP, consumption, investment, and inflation on
remittance inflow and outflow while specific objectives include to analyze the trend
and pattern of remittance inflow and outflow, and to identify the relationship between
remittance and major events.
This study is based on secondary data covering the period from 1993 to 2023.
Data have been collected from various authentic sources such as Nepal Rastra Bank,
National Statistics Office, and World Bank database. The study has employed both
descriptive, econometric and machine learning method. The Autoregressive Distributed
Lag (ARDL) model has been used to estimate relationship between remittance and
economic variables. While, a XG BOOST machine learning model has been applied
and run to test variable importance.
The findings show that remittance inflow has a positive and significant relation
on household consumption and Real GDP. Remittance outflow, though relatively
smaller, has increased gradually in past few years and shows an association with the
inflation rate. The overall result indicates that remittance inflow supports economic
growth. While, remittance outflow has a mild effect on the economy of the country.
Overall, the results of ARDL and XG BOOST find similar result. For remittance inflow
both models show the importance of consumption, where for remittance outflow both
models show the importance of inflation rate.

articles.title: Support and Preference for Grassroots Fundraising
articles.authors: Seo-young Silvia Kim; Yimeng Li
articles.abstract: Do Americans support small individual donations over other sources of political fundraising and does it matter for political behavior? Small online contributions are becoming more prevalent, and political elites and the media often idealize them as leveling the playing field in the American political ecosystem. However, we have little understanding of whether and, if so, how much the public supports small donations as a campaign funding source over others and whether such preferences translate into tangible changes in political behavior. We fill this gap with analyses of original surveys and survey experiments. Our results indicate that the public believes that there should be more small donations in American elections, fewer large individual donations, and to a much lesser extent, fewer PAC contributions. Using multiple conjoint experiments, we test whether candidates with higher dependence on small individual donors are preferred. Surprisingly, candidates relying more on small donors attract a higher likelihood of vote choice, not just within primaries or for Democrats, but across primaries, general elections, and all partisan affiliations. Such beliefs are unshaken when presented with information about lawmakers with the highest reliance on small donors, who are generally perceived as outsiders or ideologically extreme.

articles.title: Are University Journals Truly Local? National and Institutional Anchoring in Seven Research Systems
articles.authors: Maryna Nazarovets; María Fernanda Beigel; Francois van Schalkwyk; Zehra Taşkın; Ping Meng
articles.abstract: University journals (UJs) are often described as local or inward-looking, although national and institutional embeddedness are rarely distinguished. This study examines the internationally indexed segment of university journals, analysing Web of Science-indexed titles from seven countries with contrasting publishing traditions and evaluation regimes (Argentina, China, Germany, South Africa, Türkiye, Ukraine, and the United Kingdom), based on publications from 2022-2024. National anchoring (N-Anch) measures the share of papers with at least one author from the journal’s home country, while institutional anchoring (I-Anch) captures participation by authors from the publishing university. The results reveal a clear divergence between these dimensions. National anchoring is high in Türkiye, China, Ukraine, South Africa, and Argentina, but considerably lower in Germany and UK university-press journals. Institutional anchoring remains low across all countries. Thus, strong integration into a national research community does not imply institutional anchoring. The findings show that patterns of national and institutional anchoring vary substantially across countries with different research, evaluation, and publishing systems and cannot be explained by university ownership alone.

articles.title: How Much of a View Is Conveyed at Once Shapes Where Discussions Go: From Single Exchanges to Collective Belief Reorganization
articles.authors: Shinichi Honna; Takashi Hashimoto
articles.abstract: Discussions can end in a shared view, in persistent disagreement, or in little change. Such differences are usually explained by participants' initial opinions, by who interacts with whom, and by how one opinion influences another. This study examines a further, largely overlooked dimension: how much of a speaker's view is transmitted in a single contribution, which we call utterance scope. Views are not lists of independent opinions but webs of judgments about which considerations support or conflict with one another, and a contribution may transmit one such judgment or many linked judgments at once. Studying this dimension in a computational model of discussion, we find that its consequences differ across levels. In a single interaction, what matters is not how much is transmitted but how many of the receiver's judgments would actually change, and which party holds the more internally coherent view: coherent views resist revision, so an asymmetry resembling biased assimilation arises without motivated reasoning. In repeated discussion, utterance scope reshapes collective outcomes. Narrow contributions leave participants differentiated; broad contributions consolidate change into a shared direction and align remaining differences along a single axis; and new combinations of existing judgments are most abundant at intermediate scope. These differences are not explained by the total amount of change; they emerge as taken-up judgments circulate through later contributions. How much of their views people convey at a time is thus a distinct lever shaping where discussions go.

articles.title: Fiscal Federalism in Argentina, Revisited: The Dangling Thread of Municipal Governance
articles.authors: Jorge Gordin; Emilia Simison
articles.abstract: In many respects, Argentina is an antithetic case of fiscal federalism. Challenging established theses on the benefits of decentralized revenue responsibilities, it has unrelentingly grown into a textbook case of fiscal governance predicated on central government´s dominance. While significant research efforts were undertaken to decipher the roots of the resulting increase of fiscal centralization, there is a shortage of analyses exploring the role of municipal governments in such theoretical puzzle. This chapter seeks to rectify such omission, underscoring the paramount function of municipal governments as grassroots carriers of federal fiscal governance. It begins with a discussion of the theoretical state-of-the-art on local politics in federalism studies, in general, and Argentina, in particular. Next, we take a snapshot at the demographic and economic data of local governments and municipal regimes in Argentina, identifying their historical and structural underpinnings. Third, we turn our attention to the evolution and consequences of local fiscal empowerment since the 1994 Constitutional Reform. Fourth, it examines the effects and results of local governance in decisive policy areas to assess the extent to which it can be considered a critical missing link of nation-provinces relationships. In closing, we claim that despite significant strides were accomplished in advancing political decentralization in the wake of the 1994 Constitutional Reform, deepening national, provincial, and municipal triadic fiscal relations stands out as a pending assignment for further consolidating federal rule in the country.

articles.title: Hidden Labor, Hidden Harm: Gendered Trauma and the Paradox of Double Exposure in Federal Probation
articles.authors: Sandra L. Trappen; Ethan Michael Galley; Cristina Figueroa; Bobur Rakhmatullaev
articles.abstract: This U.S.-based study examines how hierarchical structures organize the emotional and relational labor of federal probation officers, shaping the institutional conditions under which justice work occurs. Drawing on a national survey of 423 officers and in‑depth interviews with 30 participants, we show how expectations of composure, distributions of relational work, and organizational norms that discourage strain disclosure create patterned vulnerabilities across the workforce. Officers in frontline roles, particularly women of color and men of color, report heightened demands and scrutiny, revealing how institutional cultures distribute emotional labor and constrain expressions of strain. Qualitative accounts illuminate the paradox of double exposure: officers are both survivors of trauma and practitioners managing others’ trauma within environments that reward stoicism and limit vulnerability. Strain emerges as the operational expression of structurally produced trauma, underscoring that trauma‑informed justice must begin with the workforce.

articles.title: Environmental Conservation or the Treadmill of Law: A Case Study of the Post-2014 Husbandry Waste Regulations in China
articles.authors: KuoRayMao; Shuqin Jin; Yu Hu; Nefratiri Weeks; Liangjun Ye
articles.abstract: As industrialized animal agriculture expanded rapidly in the last decade, the resultant pollution has generated widespread despoliation of natural resources and environmental victimization in rural China. This study examines the formulation and implementation of national environmental regulations from 2014 to 2019 and finds that the juxtaposing ministerial and provincial jurisdictions resulted in conflicting interpretations of the scale and evaluation criteria of the national policy. We argue that the regulations are more than centralized conservation programs designed to reduce environmental pollution caused by the expansion of animal husbandry. Instead, these regulations are fundamentally state-led rural development initiatives that utilize the designations of ecological protection zones to reconfigure land use and promote scale-up production in agricultural structural adjustment initiatives. The enforcement of these environmental regulations, therefore, constitutes a treadmill of law (ToL) that accelerated the geographical specialization and function intensification of the Chinese husbandry sector.

articles.title: Constrained Agency under Existential Threat: Immigrant En-trepreneurship and Expulsion
articles.authors: Robertson Khan Tengeh
articles.abstract: Structural and sociocultural constraints have long shaped African immigrant entrepreneurship in South Africa. The organised anti-foreigner campaigns of 2025–2026 echoed the earlier expulsions in Ghana (1969) and Nigeria (1983). What made them different was that the host society itself became the organised source of existential threat. This article aimed to develop a theoretical framework accounting for how entrepreneurial agency changes when organised political mobilisation simultaneously threatens physical safety, legal presence, and venture survival. The framework was developed as a conceptual model by drawing on constrained agency theory alongside scholarship on institutions, social movements, scapegoating, and moral panic. Rather than being tested with primary data, it was illustrated through historical and contemporary African cases. CAT-ET suggests that when constraints become existential, agency tends to shift towards either adaptive persistence or strategic exit. Two interacting mechanisms were specified: functional institutional inaccessibility under violence, whereby protective institutions remained operational but selectively inaccessible, and the entrepreneur-as-symbol dynamic, whereby immigrant ventures became politically constructed as emblems of economic grievance. CAT-ET reframed organised expulsion as a recurring political-economic process and offered a basis for comparative research across the Global South.

articles.title: A Blended Distribution
articles.authors: George Y. Nie
articles.abstract: We use an example to show that a distribution is asymmetric generally, arguing that a distribution in the real word is totally different from a normal distribution. Treating the force behind asymmetry as momentum, we define a distribution with momentum as a blended distribution—as if a normal distribution is disfigured by, or blended with, momentum. We propose that a variable’s movement over a period follows a distribution longitudinally whereas the literature is usually limited to a variable’s population that follows a distribution cross-sectionally. We show how the distribution of observations indicates the likelihood at a time that the variable falls within a range.

articles.title: From 4-Digit Codes to Social Class: Benchmarking Supervised Classification, Semantic Retrieval, and LLM Reranking for Multilingual Occupational Coding and Downstream Stratification (Technical report: model design, evaluation, and derived-measure accuracy)
articles.authors: Erdem YILMAZ; Elias H. Kruithof; Pieter-Paul Verhaeghe
articles.abstract: This report documents the design, implementation, and evaluation of a fully local pipeline that codes multilingual free-text occupation responses into the International Standard Classification of Occupations (ISCO-08) and derives from those codes the social-class and status measures (e.g., ESeC, ISEI, Oesch) on which much of stratification research depends. This coding is costly, slow, and only moderately consistent when done by hand. The pipeline is local (hence GDPR-friendly), reproducible, and runs on consumer-grade hardware. We benchmark and compare three approaches to the coding step: (M1) a supervised multilingual transformer classifier; (M2) semantic retrieval against a 361k-document multilingual occupation index; and (M3) the supervised classifier with an added large-language-model reranking step. On held-out European Social Survey (ESS) data the supervised classifier reaches 59.2% exact four-digit accuracy, comparable to human inter-coder agreement for this intrinsically ambiguous task, which is itself low at the four-digit level (reported by past research to be ≈42–53% between individual coders; κ ≈ 0.5 between agencies). More importantly for stratification research, given that coding errors are mostly near-misses that coarser schemes absorb, the sociologically relevant aggregate measures are recovered far more accurately, namely 80.4% for the 9-class ESeC (87.8% for its 5-class collapse), 80.5% for the 7-group ESeG, 77.9% for the 16-category Oesch scheme, and a Pearson correlation of 0.87 for the ISEI socio-economic index. The same class- and status-level accuracy holds when the model is trained and tested on canonical occupation text, so it is not an artefact of the ESS sample. Retrieval alone (M2) is substantially weaker, and contrary to the intuitive expectation, adding an LLM reranker (M3) reduces accuracy on noisy multilingual survey responses (−3.7 pp), while on clean canonical titles its effect is approximately neutral, i.e., +0.5 pp over the backbone it reranks, with no gain over the best supervised model. Instead, the supervised model’s (M1) well-calibrated confidence (ECE = 0.038) supports a human-in-the-loop workflow in which only genuinely uncertain cases are escalated to human coders. We report bootstrap confidence intervals and paired significance tests for every comparison, a train/test leakage audit, and a decomposition of geographic variation showing that the cross-country accuracy spread (in the ESS corpus) reflects response style and occupational-title ambiguity rather than language resources, whereas a genuine resource effect appears only across languages on canonical text in the normative corpus. The pipeline runs entirely offline on a single consumer-grade workstation, making automated, auditable occupation coding feasible without sending respondent data to external services.

articles.title: Locke on Money and Trust:  Between Fides, Trusteeship, and Confidence
articles.authors: JHET Assistant; Tomas Lima Pimenta
articles.abstract: This paper reinterprets the money–trust nexus in John Locke by distinguishing three rationalities of trust at work across his moral, political, and monetary writings: fides, trusteeship (fiduciary power), and confidence. Against England’s monetary turmoil of the 1690s, it reads Locke’s monetary interventions as attempts to secure public faith and contractual stability amid monetary deterioration and contested proposals to ““raise” money’s value. Fides underwrites promising and the moral intelligibility of conventional signs yet remains too fragile to sustain monetary order without reliable sanctions. Trusteeship explains why fiduciary power can secure coining, standard maintenance, and the punishment of monetary crime, but cannot create value by decree. Finally, it tackles the puzzle of “intrinsick value” by reading Locke’s universal “consent of mankind” as confidence: an impersonal trust in the persistence of a social convention, neither natural essence nor sovereign fiat.

articles.title: Career Stability and Further Training for Workers with General versus Vocational Education
articles.authors: Viktor Decker; Marco Seegers
articles.abstract: The relative merits of vocational and general education remain central to debates on sustainable careers. Vocational pathways facilitate smoother labour market entry but risk skill obsolescence, whereas general education yields weaker entry prospects but greater adaptability. A key question is whether further training can offset these trade-offs. This study examines participation in, and career stability returns to, non-formal job-related training across educational tracks. General graduates are expected to benefit more in early careers, while vocational graduates should see higher stability returns later as training counteracts skill obsolescence. Drawing on the German National Educational Panel Study, the analysis shows that secondary-level vocational graduates participate less in training than university graduates, whereas tertiary-level vocational graduates train at similar rates. Training promotes employment stability in workers’ late careers, but effects are relatively uniform across educational groups. Given uniform returns, lower participation rates disadvantage secondary-level vocational graduates relative to workers with tertiary-level qualifications.

articles.title: JUSTFAIR 2.0: A public dataset linking U.S. federal criminal sentences to the individual judges who imposed them
articles.authors: Chad M. Topaz; Maria-Veronica Ciocanel; Zofia Stanley; Christopher Thomas; Katherine Durante
articles.abstract: Federal courts sentence tens of thousands of people every year, yet the public sentencing records released by the United States Sentencing Commission (USSC) deliberately omit the identity of the sentencing judge, limiting research on and public oversight of judicial discretion. We present JUSTFAIR 2.0, a public dataset that links 140,299 federal criminal sentencing records from fiscal years 2018 through 2023 to 969 individual district judges across 87 judicial districts, using only publicly available sources. We construct the dataset in three linkage stages: (1) linkage of USSC sentencing records to case records in the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database (FJCID) using a graph-based method with offense-code similarity scoring; (2) extraction of judge identifiers embedded in docket numbers scraped from the Public Access to Court Electronic Records (PACER) system; and (3) matching of these identifiers to the Biographical Directory of Article III Federal Judges, which supplies each judge's full name, demographic information, appointment history, and appointing president. We validate the record linkage internally by comparing offense-code agreement between unique and non-unique matches (Jensen-Shannon divergence = 0.006) and validate judge matching by manually auditing a stratified sample of matches against PACER dockets, finding no errors. We document attrition at every pipeline stage and assess representativeness by comparing retained and excluded records on demographic, offense, and sentencing characteristics. The dataset updates and extends the original JUSTFAIR database, the first large-scale public resource connecting federal sentences to judges. We describe known structural limitations, including districts whose docket numbers lack judge identifiers, and offer guidance for appropriate use.

articles.title: Focused MAIHDA: Studying Intersectional Inequalities Through the Lens of a Focal Social Identity
articles.authors: George Leckie; Andrew Bell; Clare Evans
articles.abstract: Intersectional MAIHDA (Multilevel Analysis of Individual Heterogeneity and Discriminatory Accuracy) is a widely used approach in quantitative intersectional research for examining inequalities across combinations of social identity characteristics, such as gender, race, and class. However, researchers often wish to center their analysis on a single social identity characteristic, such as gender, while preserving an intersectional analytical framework. This raises questions that existing MAIHDA models cannot directly address—for example, whether the magnitude or pattern of intersectional inequalities differs by gender. To address this limitation, we propose Focused MAIHDA, a multiple-equation extension that jointly estimates subgroup-specific MAIHDA models, enabling formal comparisons of intersectional inequalities across subgroups. In doing so, we expand the range of questions that MAIHDA can address and broaden its contribution to quantitative intersectional research. We motivate and illustrate our approach by revisiting the seminal application to body mass index (BMI) by Evans et al. (2018).

articles.title: Diagnosing social norms and their influence on adolescent girls’ experience of menstruation in Khulna, Bangladesh: A theory-led qualitative exploration
articles.authors: Heather Suttor; Tasfiyah Jalil; Arifa Bente Mohosin; Erin C Hunter; Abdul Jabbar; Shampa Guha; Bithy Podder; Giorgia Gon; Sabina F. Rashid; Elissa Kennedy
articles.abstract: Menstrual health advocacy often states that harmful social norms influence adolescents' menstrual health. However, there is a lack of specificity in identifying which social norms drive menstrual behaviors and how these norms operate and are sustained. We carried out a phased qualitative study with adolescent girls in Khulna, Bangladesh, guided by Bicchieri’s (2017) social norms theory. The research team identified initial candidate behaviors, which were refined through three FGDs with mothers and five FGDs with girls. Subsequent data collection involved five FGDs with girls and three with boys, along with in-depth individual interviews (IDIs) with girls (n=15), mothers (n=7), fathers (n=3), and male (n=2) and female (n=3) teachers. Our framework analysis blended deductive coding against social norms constructs, including empirical and normative expectations, reference groups and sanctions, with inductive analysis to understand experiences. We found that a privacy norm influenced the concealment of menstruation and restricted discussions, limiting learning and support. A second influential factor was the expectation that a “good mother” teaches her daughter how to care for herself at menarche. Other behaviors, such as school attendance or care-seeking, were primarily influenced by non-normative drivers, including beliefs. Our results provide evidence and an applied theoretical framework to guide interventions. We emphasize that both empirical and normative expectations and sanctions must be identified and addressed in interventions aimed at shifting social norms. Our findings emphasize mothers and families as key reference groups and suggest interventions targeting girls alone may be unable to shift norms.

articles.title: The Social Life of R₀: Why the reproduction number is less a fact about a virus than a rumor about the society it lands in
articles.authors: Fabio Sanchez
articles.abstract: The basic reproduction number, R₀, is routinely reported as though it were an intrinsic property of a pathogen, a biological constant to be looked up and endured. It is not. R₀ is an average over a population, and its value is set largely by how that population lives: household size and age structure, density, housing and sanitation, work and mobility, and access to care. The same pathogen therefore carries different reproduction numbers across social settings, and the scalar R₀ obscures the contact structure that determines who is infected and where transmission will concentrate. None of this is news to epidemiologists; the confusion lives downstream, where a working average is repeated as though it were a fixed trait of the microbe. This essay argues that R₀ is best read not as a verdict a virus hands down but as a summary of the conditions a society arranges for it: in an outbreak, a map of where transmission will run hot; over the longer run, a lever held largely by sectors well beyond emergency response.

articles.title: Relying on the Mainstream? Entity Networks in Alternative Media
articles.authors: Paul Balluff; Hajo G. Boomgaarden; Annie Waldherr
articles.abstract: Alternative media, characterized by their heterogeneous nature and self-perceived corrective role to legacy media, have gained increasing relevance in shaping public opinion. Despite their influence, large-scale analyses of their referential and actor-related reporting characteristics remain scarce. This exploratory study investigates named entity networks in German alternative and legacy media, focusing on their reporting on the Nord Stream 2 gas pipeline from 2011 to 2022. Using computational methods, we analyze news articles from 37 alternative and 98 legacy outlets, extracting named entities and constructing co-occurrence networks to identify distinct reporting patterns. Our findings challenge assumptions that alternative media inherently diverge from legacy media in their referenced entities. While alternative media exhibit distinctive network structures—such as lower modularity and higher transitivity—they also demonstrate substantial overlap in their choice of entities and patterns of media mentions. These findings suggest that alternative media frequently mention other media, which may reflect resource limitations and reactive reporting tendencies. This study contributes to a deeper understanding of alternative media by highlighting both their unique characteristics and shared practices with legacy media.

articles.title: Arches of Discontent: The product vs feature problem of infrastructural residual space
articles.authors: Srijon Barua; Anonymous OSF
articles.abstract: In February 2019, Network Rail sold 5,261 railway arches to a Blackstone-led consortium for £1.46 billion, terminating the security of several thousand micro-enterprises, migrant traders, and arts producers. This article reads the transaction as a clarifying case of the asset-manager phase of rentier capitalism, in which publicly produced infrastructural value is converted into a securitized income stream through administrative decisions whose technical surface obscures their distributional content. Drawing on documentary analysis, site survey, and stakeholder interviews across London, Zurich, Kyoto, and Dhaka, the article identifies four institutional instruments through which infrastructural residual space is converted from feature of the urban commons to product extracted from it: discount rate methodology, rent-uplift trajectory, head-lease cascade, and statutory carve-out from security of tenure. Each of these instruments has a counterpart in regimes that produce different outcomes asking the question-what happens when infrastructure ends but the space remains? Commodity, or feature for community?

articles.title: The Social Stratification in Generative Artificial Intelligence Literacy, Use Frequency, and Workplace Acceptance in 11 European countries
articles.authors: zhuofei lu; Yao Ma
articles.abstract:
Generative AI (GenAI) has diffused rapidly across Europe, yet who feels able to
use it—and who is willing to work with it—remains poorly understood. Using the
latest CRONOS-3 panel of the probability-based European Social Survey (N =
7,556; 11 European countries, fielded in 2025), we model six separate measures
of GenAI literacy and use frequency, together with acceptance of GenAI as an
assistant and as a peer in the workplace, using country-clustered estimators with
wild-bootstrap inference. Acceptance is strongly role-differentiated: a majority
accept GenAI as an assistant, but only one in ten as a peer. Both competence and
acceptance are sharply stratified by education, age, and gender—and the gender
divide is the most consistent pattern of all: women trail men on every one of the
six literacy and use measures and on both acceptance outcomes, and the deficit
appears in behavioural use as well as in self-assessed skill, so it cannot be reduced
to gendered self-assessment alone. GenAI literacy and use frequency in turn
strongly predict acceptance in both roles. Cross-national variation is substantial,
but with only 11 countries no association between national media, scholarly, or
AI-talent environments and individual outcomes survives strict small-cluster and
multiple-testing corrections, so national context is treated descriptively. GenAI
competence and workplace acceptance thus emerge as socially stratified from the
outset—with women consistently furthest behind—an early-forming divide that
risks hardening as GenAI becomes workplace infrastructure.

articles.title: Authoritarian Environmentalism as Just Transition? A Critical Environmental Justice Examination of State Environmental Intervention in Northwestern China
articles.authors: KuoRayMao; Qian Zhang; Nefratiri Weeks
articles.abstract: Environmental justice for China’s rural populations is especially important in the context of China’s multifaceted environmental crises as existing disparities have exacerbated the unequal distribution of economic wealth and environmental harm between rural and urban communities. This chapter examines two environmental intervention programs in China to evaluate environmental justice outcomes under authoritarian environmentalism. Based on 136 in-depth interviews as well as government documents, official statistics, and reports from state-owned media in China between 2009 and 2016, our research demonstrates that the exertion of authoritarian state power in green transition may worsen environmental inequalities and dispossess the underprivileged rural populace in China. The findings indicate that just transition in China requires a multi-scalar examination on how state-led economic development initiatives and the material interests of the centralized bureaucracy shape the formulation and implementation of conservation programs and environmental regulation. We suggest that instead of viewing local communities as problems to be fixed by arbitrary administrative measures, the central state should utilize government organized NGOs affiliated with national ministries and grassroots environmental NGOs to incorporate community-based perspectives into program formulation and implementation. Institutional innovations that reconceptualize authoritarian state environmental intervention as constant responses and adjustments involving multiple stakeholders will be essential for just transitions in China and beyond.

articles.title: After the Stall: Botswana’s Resumed Fertility Decline
articles.authors: Duke Mwedzi
articles.abstract: After almost a decade of stagnation, fertility in Botswana resumed declining and is approaching replacement level. Though fertility stalls are assumed to be temporary, most of the literature has focused on explaining their causes. Less is known about how fertility changes after a stall, and register data in Botswana presents an unprecedented opportunity to study post-stall fertility with universal coverage. Using descriptive analyses and a finite mixture modelling approach, I examine the trends in childbirth between 2011 and 2023. Results show that the timing of childbirth is becoming more heterogeneous and stratified. Highly educated women are postponing first births while less educated women are accelerating them. Most children are born to unmarried mothers, and this share has increased. Fertility trends in Botswana are largely comparable to other late-transition contexts, and it may serve as an illustrative case for how other stalled countries will continue their transitions.

articles.title: Households’ regional housing affordability strain and mental health: insights from the Netherlands
articles.authors: Agata Anita Troost; Mark van Duijn
articles.abstract: Housing affordability pressures are increasingly recognised as a key determinant of mental well-being, yet existing research largely focuses on individual or household-level cost burdens, omitting the spatial context. This paper argues that housing market pressures are subject to regional market dynamics, shaping mental health in addition to individual housing affordability stress. We examine how regional housing affordability strain is associated with mental health in the Netherlands by combining LISS Panel survey data with geo-coded administrative data from Statistics Netherlands. We use a novel rank-based measure of regional price-income mismatch to capture the relative position of households within regional housing markets. Regression results show that regional housing market pressure is negatively associated with mental health in 2023, although no comparable association is found in 2018. The 2023 relationship persists after controlling for individual characteristics and household-level affordability stress. These findings suggest that the mental health consequences of the housing crisis extend beyond individual cost burdens, highlighting the importance of regional housing market dynamics as an independent source of stress.

articles.title: Beyond Interrogation: A Dialogic Autoethnography of Freedom, Security, and Competing Worldviews in Iran
articles.authors: Alibenabbas
articles.abstract:
Abstract

Social conflicts are often interpreted as disagreements over political or ideological positions. This article argues that many such conflicts emerge from deeper differences in the systems of meaning through which individuals interpret shared concepts. Using dialogic autoethnography, the study presents a composite analytical dialogue, developed from the author's lived experiences, long-term social observations, and multiple conversations within the sociopolitical context of contemporary Iran, to examine how concepts including freedom, security, justice, religion, and legitimacy acquire competing meanings within contrasting worldviews.

Rather than seeking to reconstruct a single historical conversation or privilege one political position over another, the dialogue serves as a qualitative interpretive device through which competing systems of meaning are explored. Throughout the narrative, factual, historical, legal, and social claims are supported, wherever possible, by academic scholarship and documented sources.

The dialogue progressively re-examines shared concepts through questioning and reflection, suggesting that meaningful dialogue becomes possible when the assumptions underlying apparently common concepts are made visible and reconsidered. The study proposes that durable social change depends not only on institutional transformation but also on critical reflection upon the worldviews and interpretive frameworks through which social reality is understood. Dialogic autoethnography is therefore presented as a qualitative methodological approach for exploring competing systems of meaning and facilitating reflective engagement across deeply divided perspectives.

articles.title: Gender-Based Homophily in Research:  A Large-Scale Study of Man-Woman Collaboration
articles.authors: Marek Kwiek; Wojciech Roszka
articles.abstract: We examined the male-female collaboration practices of all internationally visible Polish university professors (N = 25,463) based on their Scopus-indexed publications from 2009–2018 (158,743 journal articles). We merged a national registry of 99,935 scientists (with full administrative and biographical data) with the Scopus publication database, using probabilistic and deterministic record linkage. Our unique biographical, administrative, publication, and citation database (“The Polish Science Observatory”) included all professors with at least a doctoral degree employed in 85 research-involved universities. We determined what we term an “individual publication portfolio” for every professor, and we examined the respective impacts of biological age, academic position, academic discipline, average journal prestige, and type of institution on the same-sex collaboration ratio. The gender homophily principle (publishing predominantly with scientists of the same sex) was found to apply to male scientists—but not to females. The majority of male scientists collaborate solely with males; most female scientists, in contrast, do not collaborate with females at all. Across all age groups studied, all-female collaboration is marginal, while all-male collaboration is pervasive. Gender homophily in research-intensive institutions proved stronger for males than for females. Finally, we used a multi-dimensional fractional logit regression model to estimate the impact of gender and other individual-level and institutional-level independent variables on gender homophily in research collaboration.

articles.title: Students' Perceptions Regarding the Fairness as a Social Value (Author's English Translation)
articles.authors: Inna Gazieva
articles.abstract:
The aim of the article is to provide a sociological definition of fairness in the context of state policy to strengthen traditional Russian morals based on the results of using the author's empirical model of analyzing the students' perception regarding social values (Decree of the President of the Russian Federation No. 809 dated 11/09/2022). Methods. The theoretical and methodological basis of the research is an interdisciplinary synthesis of philosophical concepts of fairness and sociological theories of values, which made it possible to identify four dimensions of fairness value, such as ideal, desired, expected and real. Empirical testing was carried out on a representative sample of RANEPA students (N = 4338) as part of the online survey "Traditional and strategic students' values" (May-June 2023) by using a linear distribution analysis and correlation analysis (Spearman coefficient) of the sociological data. Results. The present study confirms integrity of fairness as a social value. The author revealed a high internal consistency of all its components (from the meritocratic ideal to real behavior). Furthermore, the systemic mutual relationship between fairness and responsibility, humanity, labor and cognitive activity is established. It became the basis for the operational definition of the concept under study, which now allows considering fairness not as an isolated attitude, but as the core of a value structure integrating personal and social orientations. Discussion. The author proposes a sociological definition of justice as a socially significant universal, manifested in a consistent system of attitudes and practices identified by an empirical model of social values analysis. The results are of direct practical relevance. It lies in providing an empirical model for monitoring the traditional value interiorization among young people and developing value education focused not on declarative assimilation of norms, but on the formation of an internally consistent value position that can become the basis for building a just society by means of personal responsibility and ethic interaction.

Author's English translation of the article published in Russian: Central Russian Journal of Social Sciences, 2026, vol. 21, no. 1, pp. 81-99 (EDN RQSSEN). The Russian original is the version of record. Archived version of this translation: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21509404

articles.title: Value Basis of the Professional Potential of Students: Research Methodology (Author's English Translation)
articles.authors: Inna Gazieva
articles.abstract:
This article attempts to solve the problem of developing and applying a value-based approach to the formation of the professional potential of students, which is manifested in the contradiction between the need for a scientific approach to the formation of the professional potential of students, ensuring the stability of the state socio-professional reproduction system and its personnel sovereignty, and the lack of a scientific and methodological base sufficient for its study and subsequent formation. The purpose of this article is to describe the author's methodology for studying the value basis of the professional potential of students, as well as the results of its testing. The empirical basis of the study was the results of a sociological survey conducted by the author based on an empirical model of the analysis of the professional potential of students developed earlier (students of universities and branches in 36 regions of the Russian Federation; N = 3864); the data analysis was carried out using the descriptive statistics method. The article analyzes the attitude of students to the terminal and instrumental values of society declared by the state, which form the basis of the professional potential of students as their desired image, which, depending on the level of internalization, are distributed among structural levels. In addition, the article suggests a scheme for assessing the professional potential of students, which is a calculation of the integral indicator of the formation of two groups of values: terminal and instrumental. The article concludes that the value basis of the professional potential of students is very heterogeneous, which is explained by the specifics of the implementation of youth policy, while at the same time determining the prospects for its implementation. The proposed methodology can be used both during further study of the country's student youth and can be expanded to other socio-professional groups.

Author's English translation of the article published in Russian: Vestnik of Saint Petersburg University. Sociology, 2025, vol. 18, iss. 3, pp. 284-301 (EDN LPWJHD). The Russian original is the version of record. Archived version of this translation: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21508549

articles.title: The young and the old, the fast and the slow: a large-scale study of productivity classes and rank advancement
articles.authors: Marek Kwiek; Wojciech Roszka
articles.abstract: We examined a large sample of Polish science, technology, engineering, mathematics, and medicine (STEMM) scientists (N = 16,083) to study rank advancement and productivity in the past 40 years. We used two previously neglected time dimensions – promotion age and promotion speed – to construct individual lifetime biographical and publication profiles. We followed a classificatory approach and the new methodological approach of journal prestige–normalized productivity. All scientists were allocated to different productivity, promotion age, and promotion speed classes (top 20%, middle 60%, and bottom 20%). The patterns found were consistent across all disciplines: scientists in young promotion age classes (and fast promotion speed classes) in the past were currently the most productive. In contrast, scientists in old promotion age classes (and slow promotion speed classes) in the past were currently the least productive. In the three largest disciplines, the young-old promotion age productivity differential for associate professors was 100–200% (150–200% for full professors), and the fast-slow promotion speed productivity differential for associate professors was 80–150% (100–170% for full professors).
